questions.title: Move the calculation boundary before the pilot
questions.stem: A tunnel survey team proposes a model that converts surveyor notes into both a narrative and a clearance verdict. Clearance is defined by a published deterministic formula using calibrated sensor readings. Reviewers can approve narratives, but the automated verdict immediately releases equipment and cannot wait for review. A prototype reproduces ninety-nine historical verdicts correctly. Which architectural recommendation BEST addresses the fit of this proposed release boundary?

options.text: Keep clearance in validated calculation code and evaluate a separate, source-linked narrative assistant under the existing review process.
options.why: The release requires exact reproducible computation without review; strong historical agreement does not justify moving that boundary into generation.

options.text: Convert the formula into few-shot worked examples and restrict outputs to the two allowed clearance verdict labels.
options.why: Examples and constrained labels improve presentation but still leave the critical calculation to probabilistic generation rather than validated code.

options.text: Use the historical prototype as a release filter, escalating only survey notes unlike those in the ninety-nine examples.
options.why: Similarity to observed notes cannot establish the correctness of a new safety-relevant numeric calculation or its unreviewed release.

options.text: Retain model-generated verdicts but require two independently worded prompts to agree before the automatic equipment release proceeds.
options.why: Agreement can repeat a shared computational mistake and does not establish the formula execution guarantee required at the release boundary.

questions.decision: The fit decision concerns the consequence and mechanism, rather than a favorable aggregate score. Preserve exact clearance computation in code and use language generation for the reviewable explanation. The historical test remains useful evidence for that narrower assistant, not authorization to replace the release calculation.

video_evidence.concept: Deterministic safety-critical calculations are a poor unchecked LLM fit

questions.title: Establish a minimal diagnostic baseline
questions.stem: A botanical garden needs one sentence describing each exhibition from three curator-supplied facts. There are no live tools, the facts fit in a short prompt, and a human selects the sentence. A proposed architecture adds fact extraction, planning, drafting and critique agents before any baseline exists. The curator provides an acceptance rubric covering all three facts and tone. Which first experiment BEST tests the simplest viable implementation?

options.text: Start with a critic loop limited to one revision, because a bounded loop is the smallest acceptable production architecture.
options.why: A bound controls loop exposure but does not establish that any loop adds value over a sufficient single call.

options.text: Compare one explicitly instructed prompt against the curator rubric, reserving orchestration for demonstrated failure classes that simpler changes cannot fix.
options.why: The task is bounded and supplied with sufficient evidence; measuring the minimal baseline establishes whether orchestration has any necessary purpose.

options.text: Collect a training corpus of curator-approved sentences before testing prompts, so stylistic consistency is guaranteed in the first pilot.
options.why: Corpus preparation delays the lowest-cost diagnostic experiment and training data cannot guarantee the required behavior on unseen descriptions.

options.text: Implement extraction and drafting agents first, measuring their final output before deciding whether the other proposed agents are necessary.
options.why: This assumes an unnecessary decomposition before measuring whether a single call already satisfies the bounded drafting requirement.

questions.decision: A minimal baseline is an experiment with an explicit acceptance rule. Here the supplied facts, short output and human selection make a single call plausible. Add architectural machinery only when measured failures identify a need and a comparison demonstrates enough improvement to justify its overhead.

video_evidence.concept: Try the simplest viable prompt before orchestration

questions.title: Feedback must change a tested release
questions.stem: A restoration assistant receives correction notes from conservators. Its dashboard already counts them, but the same unsupported varnish claims recur after every deployment. Privacy-approved excerpts can be retained for evaluation; original production records cannot be reused directly. The team wants a feedback loop rather than an additional runtime filter. Which TWO changes most directly close the loop from observed failure to a verified shared improvement?

options.text: Expand retrieval for every request so a greater number of conservation passages accompany the unchanged prompt revision.
options.why: This changes runtime context without establishing why the claim failed or verifying that feedback produced an effective correction.

options.text: Send each correction back into the originating conversation and mark the production feedback ticket resolved after acknowledgment.
options.why: Acknowledgment can improve one exchange but does not demonstrate a shared release improvement or prevent recurrence for other conservators.

options.text: Add a dashboard showing correction counts by conservator and close the review cycle once the trend becomes visible.
options.why: Visibility supports diagnosis but counting alone does not create a tested behavioral change in the production assistant.

options.text: Turn approved correction excerpts into adjudicated regression cases that preserve the mistaken claim and the required evidence boundary.
options.why: Regression cases convert permitted observations into reproducible criteria that can reveal whether the same failure survives a proposed change.

options.text: Require candidate prompt revisions to pass those cases and a representative holdout before recording and deploying the new version.
options.why: A tested release connects the feedback signal to changed behavior while checking that a narrow repair does not break ordinary work.

questions.decision: A feedback loop needs an evidence-to-change path. Derive permitted regression material, adjudicate the desired behavior, and test a candidate release with broader coverage before deployment. Counting complaints or repairing isolated chats supplies observations but leaves the shared failure mechanism unchanged.

video_evidence.concept: Feedback turns outcomes into evaluations and tested updates

questions.title: Validate extracted usability before expensive work
questions.stem: A geological archive accepts raster maps for an assistant that cites coordinates. A new upload passes the extension and byte-size checks, yet the ingest worker extracts a blank image because the file advertises dimensions inconsistent with its decoded payload. Generation then invents place names. The owner requires readable map evidence or a repairable rejection. Which additional input boundary BEST prevents this failure before model invocation?

options.text: Provide a map-reading uncertainty instruction and permit generation whenever the upstream upload returned a successful storage identifier.
options.why: Storage success only establishes persistence and cannot substitute for validation that the model receives readable coordinate evidence.

options.text: Run a second model to assess the first generated place names and reject output if the two models disagree.
options.why: Downstream disagreement checking spends inference on unusable input and may still accept mutually plausible invented geography without source evidence.

options.text: Decode with bounded resource limits, verify expected readable content and dimensions, then reject or request repair when the evidence is unusable.
options.why: Checking the actual decoded representation catches the observed mismatch and gives a concrete input failure state before unsupported generation begins.

options.text: Lower the accepted file-size limit until every currently failing map is excluded, preserving the existing extension-based validation path.
options.why: A smaller file can contain the same malformed representation; byte size is not proof that usable map content was extracted.

questions.decision: Validate the representation the downstream stage will actually consume. A successful upload is insufficient when decoding can fail or exhaust resources. Bounded decoding and content checks establish a useful input contract, with a clear repair route instead of asking a model to recover missing evidence.

video_evidence.concept: Validate type size and readability before model processing

questions.title: Gate the intermediate contract
questions.stem: A public-audio producer creates a single coherent episode script from interview evidence. Every script must address consent, attribution and pronunciation before recording, but final prose checks sometimes find missing material after costly voice rendering. Writers can provide a structured outline containing source handles for each obligation. Which workflow BEST enforces the prerequisites early while preserving coherent writing and avoiding an unnecessary specialist-agent decomposition?

options.text: Draft the script once and ask the model to append any missing obligations immediately before beginning voice rendering.
options.why: An unchecked self-assessment may miss the same obligation and provides no explicit validated intermediate contract for subsequent work.

options.text: Route each interview to a dedicated style prompt, then perform the existing mandatory-section check after voice rendering completes.
options.why: Routing can improve specialization but leaves the observed prerequisite failure undetected until the same expensive downstream stage.

options.text: Write each mandatory obligation in parallel and concatenate the sections, using a transition prompt only if the producer complains.
options.why: Independent section generation risks inconsistency and does not enforce the evidence-linked plan needed for a coherent complete episode.

options.text: Generate an evidence-linked outline, validate all required obligations in code, then draft one script and recheck the final artifact.
options.why: An intermediate deterministic gate prevents expensive drafting from proceeding on an incomplete plan while final checking covers later omissions.

questions.decision: Use prompt chaining where a validated intermediate artifact creates a meaningful gate. Check the outline against explicit obligations before expensive downstream work, then verify the final script too. Passing a plan does not guarantee that generation preserves it; the two checks protect distinct stage boundaries.

video_evidence.concept: Prompt chaining supports programmatic intermediate gates

questions.title: Value alone does not establish agent viability
questions.stem: A freight cooperative considers an agent that investigates contradictory routing notices. The branches genuinely vary and resolving a case is valuable. However, the prototype has no machine-readable acknowledgment from the booking service, so it cannot distinguish a successful reservation from a timeout after commit. Duplicate reservations incur penalties. Which conclusion BEST applies agent suitability checks before authorizing autonomous retries in this environment?

options.text: Treat reliable action feedback as an unresolved viability condition and repair acknowledgment or idempotency before autonomous booking retries are permitted.
options.why: Complexity and value support investigation, but missing action-state evidence makes the consequential retry loop operationally unsafe under the stated costs.

options.text: Authorize retries because the investigation branches cannot be enumerated, using an overall spending cap to bound duplicate-booking penalties.
options.why: A cap limits total exposure without resolving whether a retry duplicates an already committed reservation or satisfies the business requirement.

options.text: Select a stronger reasoning configuration and use its inferred booking status whenever the service response fails to arrive.
options.why: Reasoning cannot recover authoritative commit state absent service evidence; this substitutes a plausible guess for the missing action feedback.

options.text: Approve the agent after comparing average reservation speed with the manual baseline, treating rare duplicates as an optimization backlog.
options.why: Speed comparison omits the stated error cost and unresolved viability boundary that must be addressed before autonomous consequential retries.

questions.decision: Agent suitability includes whether the environment supplies trustworthy feedback for the next action. Variable work and high value are insufficient when commit state is unknowable and repetition has consequences. Repair the interface or keep that action under a controlled workflow before expanding agent autonomy.

video_evidence.concept: Agent suitability includes complexity value viability and tolerable error cost

questions.title: Separate critique from persuasive history
questions.stem: A scientific caption generator includes a detailed defense of why every draft satisfies the rubric. Its critic sees that defense, the rubric and the draft, and overlooks unsupported causal language. The critic must check evidence because an awkward-looking caption may still be correct. Which TWO changes best reduce anchoring while preserving the information needed for substantive independent critique rather than merely making the critic more negative?

options.text: Keep the complete author context and instruct the critic to reject a fixed fraction of captions from every batch.
options.why: A rejection quota can manufacture apparent scrutiny without improving evidence-sensitive detection of the causal error identified in the scenario.

options.text: Give the critic the draft, rubric and relevant source evidence in a fresh context without the generator’s self-justifying conversation.
options.why: Removing persuasive author history reduces anchoring while retaining the independent evidence necessary to judge the actual causal claims.

options.text: Validate critic discrimination on adjudicated captions with and without subtle causal overstatements before using its verdict as a revision gate.
options.why: Measured discrimination establishes whether the redesigned reviewer catches the targeted defect rather than merely changing its overall rejection frequency.

options.text: Ask the generator to summarize its defense more concisely and place that summary immediately before the critic’s final verdict.
options.why: A shorter persuasive rationale still anchors review and does not create an independent evaluation of the submitted caption against evidence.

options.text: Hide the source excerpts as well as the author history so the critic’s judgment cannot be influenced by any shared information.
options.why: Independence does not mean withholding task evidence; a critic cannot assess factual support reliably when denied the relevant source material.

questions.decision: Independent evaluation requires a clean judgment context, not informational blindness. Supply the artifact, criteria and source evidence while excluding the author’s advocacy. Then measure the reviewer on known defects and valid outputs. A higher rejection rate alone is not evidence that criticism has become more accurate.

video_evidence.concept: Critics need independent context rather than generator reasoning

questions.title: Trace the transformation between specialists
questions.stem: A landscape-history system combines specialist findings into a final chronology. Specialists return source-backed dates, but a synthesis step normalizes ambiguous calendar notation and sometimes introduces the wrong year. Operators can identify the worker source but cannot tell whether the year changed during normalization or final writing. Which THREE trace additions most directly make the introduced claim attributable without requiring unrestricted storage of every underlying document?

options.text: Assign stable claim identifiers and record parent claim links whenever normalization derives a new chronology statement from specialist results.
options.why: A derivation edge identifies which earlier assertion produced the transformed claim, distinguishing worker evidence from a downstream interpretation.

options.text: Attach final chronology statements to their derived claim identifiers and retain controlled source handles under the approved evidence policy.
options.why: Final-to-derived linkage completes attribution across synthesis while controlled handles avoid making every raw historical document an unrestricted trace payload.

options.text: Preserve each specialist’s final report and the published chronology, correlating changed dates by nearest matching text at incident time.
options.why: Text similarity can suggest an origin but cannot reliably reconstruct which transformation or assumption introduced a specific changed year.

options.text: Record the normalizer version, explicit calendar assumption and resulting value alongside the input claim identifier for each transformed date.
options.why: These fields expose the specific transformation responsible for a changed year and support focused reproduction of the disputed derivation.

options.text: Record only the specialist name against every published statement, since source-backed worker findings already establish end-to-end provenance.
options.why: Attributing the statement to its worker hides the downstream normalizer that may have introduced the erroneous year during synthesis.

questions.decision: Orchestrator observability must cover transformations as well as worker returns. Record derivation links, transformation versions and relevant assumptions, then connect published statements to those records. This extends the chapter’s worker-provenance lesson to synthesis lineage; it is an application design, not a claim that a platform supplies it automatically.

video_evidence.concept: Orchestrator logs must preserve task output and source provenance

questions.title: Freeze the shared semantic contract
questions.stem: A cultural catalogue project divides audio annotation by recording. Annotators agree on ordinary instrument names but disagree about whether a historic name means a modern instrument family or a specific object. A curator can approve a disambiguation table. Recordings remain independently processable, and the table may change after review. Which TWO decomposition requirements best prevent internally inconsistent catalogue releases while retaining parallel annotation?

options.text: Run an integration audit for conflicting identifiers and flag batches requiring reprocessing when a material vocabulary revision changes interpretation.
options.why: The audit verifies the shared dependency after parallel work and exposes where updated terminology invalidates earlier annotations rather than hiding inconsistency.

options.text: Translate the disputed name into a common language before annotation and treat the translated spelling as the canonical identity.
options.why: Translation can preserve the same ambiguity and does not establish the curator’s domain distinction between an instrument family and an object.

options.text: Bind each annotation batch to a curator-approved vocabulary revision containing the distinctions and evidence rules required by all workers.
options.why: A shared versioned semantic contract makes independently processed recordings comparable and prevents silent mixing of different term interpretations.

options.text: Let each recording worker choose the best historic interpretation and have the final writer normalize the visible spelling only.
options.why: Matching surface spelling does not resolve different object meanings, so apparently uniform labels can still encode incompatible catalogue identities.

options.text: Give every worker all completed annotations from earlier recordings so later workers gradually converge on the majority interpretation.
options.why: Sequential majority anchoring is neither a curator-approved semantic contract nor a guarantee that early and late batches use the same meaning.

questions.decision: Decomposition needs a shared dependency contract where independent tasks interpret the same terms. Freeze its revision per batch and audit integration for semantic conflicts. When the contract changes, identify affected outputs explicitly; consistency is about stable meaning and evidence, not simply identical surface words.

video_evidence.concept: Decomposition shares terminology then checks consistency

questions.title: Remove only the unsupported decomposition
questions.stem: A logistics helpdesk uses four sequential model stages. The first three derive routing labels and prose that a fourth stage rewrites. A deterministic eligibility check and human approval occur outside those stages. In a paired evaluation, one model call matches the four-stage process on every required quality slice and cuts elapsed time by sixty percent. Which simplification BEST follows while preserving the existing non-model obligations?

options.text: Retain four stages but share one conversation across them so caching can reproduce the measured single-call latency reduction.
options.why: A shared conversation does not remove sequential dependencies and has not demonstrated the single-call candidate’s measured latency or quality behavior.

options.text: Replace the four model stages with the evaluated single call while retaining eligibility and approval gates in the surrounding workflow.
options.why: The evidence supports collapsing redundant generation stages, while the independent mandatory controls remain obligations unaffected by that equivalence result.

options.text: Keep only the first stage and remove the final writer, assuming any reduction in call count preserves the measured quality result.
options.why: The evaluated candidate was a specific single-call design; arbitrary stage removal does not inherit its observed quality equivalence.

options.text: Replace the entire workflow with the single call because matching output quality establishes equivalence of all production controls.
options.why: Output comparisons do not demonstrate that the model enforces deterministic eligibility or obtains the separately required human approval.

questions.decision: Match decomposition to demonstrated need. Remove the stages shown to add no quality value, but preserve control obligations outside that comparison. The chapter supports simplifying generation overhead; it does not justify erasing deterministic or human gates that were held constant during the evaluation.

video_evidence.concept: Collapse unnecessary model stages when a simpler call matches quality

questions.title: Measure the residual review burden
questions.stem: A procurement assistant is funded to save analyst time. Before deployment, 2,000 monthly cases require twelve analyst minutes each. The proposed design uses two minutes for every case plus an additional eight minutes for thirty percent escalated to specialists. All time is additive, and case volume is unchanged. Quality gates pass. What efficiency statement correctly informs the sponsor before deciding whether the additional review fits the business case?

options.text: Expected analyst work becomes 8,000 minutes monthly, a 66.7 percent reduction, by averaging the two review stages equally.
options.why: An equal weighting is unsupported by the stated escalation probability and does not calculate the additive expected per-case workload.

options.text: Expected analyst work falls to 4,800 minutes monthly, an eighty percent reduction, because only escalated cases consume review time.
options.why: This counts the additional specialist time but omits the two minutes incurred for every case, understating total human work.

options.text: Expected analyst work falls to 8,800 minutes monthly, a 63.3 percent reduction, subject to confirming the stated escalation rate in operation.
options.why: Each case averages 2 + 0.30 × 8 = 4.4 minutes; comparison with twelve baseline minutes gives the stated reduction.

options.text: Expected analyst work becomes 20,000 minutes monthly, a 16.7 percent reduction, because every case requires both review stages.
options.why: This applies the extra eight minutes to all cases even though only thirty percent escalate under the stipulated workload.

questions.decision: Use the complete review workload: 2,000 × (2 + 0.30 × 8) = 8,800 minutes versus 24,000 baseline minutes. The saving is 15,200/24,000 = 63.33 percent. Confirm escalation frequency and quality after deployment before translating saved time into an unrelated cash or staffing claim.

video_evidence.concept: Business value decisions expose accuracy and efficiency tradeoffs

questions.title: Evaluate the suggestion that is still current
questions.stem: A typing assistant uses a high-capability model selected for excellent completed-suggestion quality. In realistic sessions, seventy percent of requests become obsolete before their suggestion arrives because the user keeps typing. A faster, cheaper supported tier has not been evaluated on this workload. The owner values accepted suggestions tied to the current document revision. Which next evaluation BEST tests model fit without treating completed-output quality as sufficient evidence for the interactive feature?

options.text: Choose the cheapest tier immediately and report its advertised throughput as proof that suggestions will arrive before subsequent user edits.
options.why: Tier reputation does not establish this workload’s timely acceptance quality; the candidate needs an end-to-end comparison under realistic revision changes.

options.text: Keep the current model because its completed suggestions score highest, excluding canceled requests from all cost and usefulness calculations.
options.why: Completed-output quality omits most real requests here, and ignoring obsolete work hides the cost and experience implications of the current model choice.

options.text: Evaluate the faster tier on saved static documents only, measuring grammatical quality while preserving the current session cancellation rate as a fixed assumption.
options.why: Static outputs omit the interaction timing that motivates the selection and cannot establish the faster configuration’s actual revision-valid suggestion acceptance rate.

options.text: Compare configurations on current-revision suggestion acceptance and end-to-end arrival time, including canceled work and total expense under realistic typing sessions.
options.why: The evaluation measures useful timely suggestions and wasted work, making speed and quality tradeoffs visible for the actual interactive workload.

questions.decision: Model fit depends on useful output within the interaction window. Evaluate the faster tier against current-revision acceptance, timing and total expense including canceled work. This applies the chapter’s latency-sensitive selection lesson without promising a named tier always meets a deadline or confusing static quality with interactive success.

video_evidence.concept: Latency-sensitive model selection needs measured task quality and speed

questions.title: Retain eligibility through a fallback
questions.stem: A legal research service has a contract requiring zero retention for covered client payloads. Compliance approved route A for that scope. Engineers add route B as an automatic overload fallback, based on stronger benchmark results, but have not checked whether the selected model and endpoint are eligible under the agreement. Compliance owns contractual determinations. Which TWO changes correctly preserve the requirement before the fallback handles those payloads?

options.text: Set the fallback’s reasoning effort lower and remove debug logging, treating these settings as proof that provider retention is disabled.
options.why: Local logging and reasoning settings do not establish provider retention terms for the selected model, endpoint and feature combination.

options.text: Require documented model-and-feature eligibility approval for route B under the actual agreement before adding it to the permitted fallback set.
options.why: Retention eligibility depends on the actual route and scope; a stronger benchmark or organization-level agreement does not independently establish coverage.

options.text: Enable route B only for the shortest client requests because small payloads create a proportionately smaller retention obligation.
options.why: Payload length does not change the stipulated zero-retention requirement or establish eligibility of an otherwise unapproved processing route.

options.text: Keep route B disabled during normal traffic but permit it during overload because emergency availability is an implied contract exception.
options.why: No emergency exception is stipulated; runtime overload cannot supply the contractual authorization that compliance has not established.

options.text: Make routing reject ineligible fallbacks and test overload behavior with an explicit unavailable response or an already approved alternative.
options.why: An enforced route policy preserves the contractual boundary when the primary fails rather than silently prioritizing availability over approved processing conditions.

questions.decision: Treat retention eligibility as a routing constraint, including degraded modes. Verify the actual agreement with its owner and enforce the approved model, endpoint and feature set in code. Current covered-model restrictions have exceptions, so neither universal coverage nor universal exclusion should replace route-specific contractual evidence.

video_evidence.concept: Model selection and zero-retention eligibility must be assessed together

questions.title: Specify the audience without hiding uncertainty
questions.stem: A radiology research assistant serves specialists comparing published imaging studies. The prompt only says to be helpful, so every answer explains elementary imaging terminology and buries study limitations. Researchers need concise comparisons but still want explanations of unfamiliar methods when requested. No patient advice is provided. Which prompt revision BEST establishes the audience and useful depth without introducing a blanket ban that would suppress legitimate clarification?

options.text: Define specialist readers, prioritize study differences and limitations, and explain unfamiliar terms when the request or evidence context makes that useful.
options.why: An explicit audience and task hierarchy targets the missing context while preserving explanations that actually help specialists interpret a study.

options.text: Specify a fixed maximum sentence length and delete all terminology definitions from the prompt examples used by the assistant.
options.why: Sentence length does not establish reader expertise and deleting definitions indiscriminately can remove useful support for unfamiliar methods.

options.text: Give researchers a verbosity slider and leave the shared prompt unchanged so every user can shorten basic explanations individually.
options.why: A length control may reduce output but leaves the missing audience assumptions and the priority of study limitations unaddressed.

options.text: Assign a prestigious specialist role and ask for maximal sophistication, leaving the relative importance of limitations and definitions unstated.
options.why: A status label without audience and task priorities can increase jargon while leaving the observed information-ordering problem unresolved.

questions.decision: Role instructions work best when they specify who reads the answer and which decisions the answer supports. Define the specialist audience, prioritize comparison and limitations, and allow useful clarification. This is an evaluated communication contract, not a claim that naming an expert role guarantees factual expertise.

video_evidence.concept: Audience and role instructions determine explanation depth

questions.title: Replace a ban with a usable form
questions.stem: A community radio tool writes notices for presenters who read directly from a teleprompter. Its instruction says never use lists, abbreviations or symbols, yet notices still contain compact fragments that are difficult to speak. The production contract requires a complete spoken notice including the event, date, venue and cancellation condition. Which revised instruction BEST tells the assistant the positive behavior to produce without relying on a growing catalogue of forbidden characters?

options.text: Enumerate every recently observed symbol and abbreviation in the negative rule, preserving the current unspecified output form for flexibility.
options.why: The expanded prohibition still leaves the intended spoken form unstated and can chase surface variations without fixing the communication contract.

options.text: Write a natural spoken paragraph using complete sentences, pronounceable dates and all four required facts, then check it against the broadcast rubric.
options.why: The instruction defines the desired modality and content rather than expecting the model to infer a speakable notice from formatting prohibitions.

options.text: Add a final self-review asking whether the output violates any existing ban, without changing the original notice-generation instructions.
options.why: A self-review against the same negative contract does not specify the complete positive spoken form the presenters actually need.

options.text: Require plain text with no markup and use a smaller output token cap so compact fragments cannot continue for long.
options.why: Plain text can contain unspeakable fragments, and truncation risks removing the cancellation condition rather than producing natural spoken sentences.

questions.decision: Say what a successful artifact looks like: a spoken paragraph, complete sentences, pronounceable values and required facts. Test those criteria directly. Positive formatting guidance addresses the chapter’s lesson while the broadcast rubric remains necessary to establish that the actual output is usable.

video_evidence.concept: Positive instructions communicate the desired output form

questions.title: Separate demonstrations from live evidence
questions.stem: A repair classifier receives several solved demonstrations followed by a real work order. Some demonstration text contains nested quotation marks and the phrase current request. The model occasionally classifies the example instead of the work order. Examples demonstrably improve borderline classifications, so removing them loses quality. Which TWO prompt-construction changes best preserve the examples while clarifying their role and preventing accidental structural confusion?

options.text: Mark the entire combined prompt as trusted XML so the model treats every phrase inside the examples as higher-priority instructions.
options.why: Markup separates content roles but is not a trust boundary; elevating example text would worsen the confusion about instructions and evidence.

options.text: Move the solved demonstrations after the live work order and rely on their later position to establish that they are historical.
options.why: Position alone does not label instructional versus live content and may make the examples more salient without resolving their role.

options.text: Escape or encode delimiter-like content when rendering records and test examples containing the same boundary tokens as production input.
options.why: Structural handling prevents record text from accidentally closing or imitating containers; adversarial boundary fixtures verify the actual prompt renderer.

options.text: Render demonstrations in a labeled examples container and place the live work order in a distinct task-input container with explicit instructions.
options.why: Separate labeled roles distinguish instructional examples from the actual object to classify without discarding the demonstrated benefit of examples.

options.text: Rename all demonstration customers to Example and keep the same unmarked concatenation of examples and the production work order.
options.why: A shared placeholder reduces name variety but does not establish structural boundaries or stop the live and demonstration records being confused.

questions.decision: Examples need explicit roles and sound rendering. Separate demonstrations from live input, and ensure content cannot accidentally impersonate the delimiters used by the template. These measures clarify context organization; they do not turn XML into a security boundary or make untrusted record text authoritative.

video_evidence.concept: Clearly marked examples must remain separate from actual input

questions.title: Preserve the visual detail that matters
questions.stem: A ceramics cataloguer sends sixteen shelf photographs to read a maker’s mark on one selected object. A pilot locates the object reliably, but a proposed uniform thumbnail resize makes the tiny mark illegible. The application may crop the original locally before the model call. Which input policy BEST reduces irrelevant visual tokens while retaining the evidence needed for this specific recognition task and avoiding unsupported assumptions about image-link pricing?

options.text: Keep all sixteen full images and lower the maximum output tokens so the total image-processing cost falls without changing recognition quality.
options.why: The output ceiling does not reduce already supplied image input tokens and may truncate the uncertainty statement needed for unclear marks.

options.text: Resize every shelf image to the smallest common thumbnail and recover unclear marks through a stronger reasoning configuration.
options.why: Reasoning cannot restore visual details removed by resizing; the proposal sacrifices the evidence required to distinguish the maker’s mark.

options.text: Send a context thumbnail plus a sufficiently detailed crop of the selected mark, then verify recognition and abstention on difficult examples.
options.why: Targeted cropping preserves task-relevant detail while reducing irrelevant shelf content; evaluation establishes whether the new representation remains adequate for identification.

options.text: Send all sixteen originals as URL image sources because remote references avoid the input-token charge associated with uploaded images.
options.why: A supported image URL still supplies processed visual input and does not make the image content free of token usage.

questions.decision: Optimize visual input around the actual recognition evidence. A contextual view and detailed crop can remove irrelevant pixels without destroying the mark. Measure both successful reading and appropriate abstention. Actual visual token behavior depends on model processing and caps, so larger source files do not imply indefinitely growing charges.

video_evidence.concept: Relevant image selection and resolution control visual input cost

questions.title: Keep source identity through comparison
questions.stem: A heritage researcher compares three editions of a field guide. They share titles and paragraph numbering but disagree about one identification rule. The context builder concatenates extracted text, discarding edition dates and source handles. Answers blend clauses into a rule that appears in no edition. Which TWO changes best improve document organization and evidential comparison while keeping the question grounded in the supplied editions rather than relying on general model knowledge?

options.text: Give each document a distinct container with edition identity, date and stable source handle, preserving those fields through extraction.
options.why: Separate identity-bearing context prevents identical paragraph numbers or titles from erasing which edition supplies a rule or qualification.

options.text: Remove dates to avoid recency bias and ask the model to choose the interpretation that sounds most internally consistent.
options.why: The task requires edition-specific differences; discarding identity and optimizing plausibility further weakens evidence attribution rather than restoring it.

options.text: Summarize each document without its source metadata and combine the summaries into one authoritative reference passage for every future question.
options.why: Unlabeled summaries preserve the attribution loss and may turn a comparison of conflicting editions into an unsupported universal rule.

options.text: Deduplicate paragraphs with the same number before generation, preferring the longest variant as the most complete formulation of the rule.
options.why: Matching paragraph numbers across editions do not imply equivalent content; deduplication can erase exactly the disagreement the researcher wants explained.

options.text: Ask for edition-specific supporting passages before synthesizing differences, and verify every comparative claim against its referenced edition.
options.why: Evidence-first comparison makes conflicting source boundaries visible and gives the final synthesis an inspectable basis rather than an invented blended rule.

questions.decision: Long context requires source identity as well as text. Preserve edition metadata, isolate documents and demand evidence for each comparison. Quoting or referencing the source before synthesis helps expose conflicts, but still requires checking; well-formed containers alone do not establish that a generated claim is supported.

video_evidence.concept: Document containers and metadata prevent cross-document clause mixing

questions.title: Find the first changing cache dependency
questions.stem: A shared assistant caches its system manual. Each tenant has identical tool behavior, yet the application reorders JSON property descriptions and inserts a tenant display name into tool metadata before the system block. Requests arrive frequently, exceed the model’s cache minimum and have sufficient lifetime. Which TWO changes directly address the earliest prefix mismatch while preserving tenant-specific authorization in the application rather than hiding it inside cached instructions?

options.text: Remove tools from the request and include their definitions in a system appendix, leaving tool execution unchanged in the client.
options.why: Textual descriptions are not equivalent executable tool definitions and do not preserve the established integration contract merely by moving their wording.

options.text: Keep tenant authorization enforced outside cached text and compare cache creation and read usage across otherwise identical controlled requests.
options.why: Application enforcement preserves access boundaries while usage measurements establish whether stabilizing the actual prefix improved cache reuse as expected.

options.text: Make tool definitions deterministic and tenant-independent, moving display-only tenant information into the variable request content after the reusable prefix.
options.why: The cache hierarchy begins with tools, so changing upstream definitions prevents reuse of the following system content even when the manual matches.

options.text: Move the cache breakpoint to the end of each tenant-specific tool description so the service automatically factors out all stable words.
options.why: A breakpoint still covers the preceding changed content; it does not rewrite varying definitions into a common reusable prefix.

options.text: Raise the cache lifetime while preserving per-tenant tool mutations because frequent arrivals show the only remaining cause is expiry.
options.why: The stipulated mismatch occurs before the manual and cannot be repaired by retaining a cache entry whose prefix does not match.

questions.decision: Diagnose the earliest changing dependency in the tools-to-system-to-messages prefix. Stabilize equivalent tool definitions, keep variable display data later and verify usage. Caching is a computation reuse mechanism; tenant authorization must remain an enforced application property regardless of whether cached instructions are shared.

video_evidence.concept: Changing tool definitions invalidates later system prefix caching

questions.title: Consolidate aliases without widening authority
questions.stem: A studio exposes four catalogue tools with overlapping descriptions. Trace analysis shows two are genuine aliases, while the other two search unpublished assets and archived assets under different access policies. The model often repeats the alias calls. The owner wants less capability confusion without creating a general search operation that silently crosses asset states. Which redesign BEST removes accidental overlap while retaining the meaningful business boundaries?

options.text: Keep every tool but prepend a universal instruction to prefer the first tool whenever multiple catalogue operations appear suitable.
options.why: An arbitrary preference retains duplicate surface area and can select the wrong access-state operation rather than resolving actual semantic overlap.

options.text: Merge all four into one search operation whose state argument defaults to every state, relying on results to explain access differences.
options.why: A broad default expands the common task’s authority and obscures the distinct state boundaries that the owner explicitly needs preserved.

options.text: Hide all tool descriptions behind search and keep the duplicate names because deferred definitions eliminate selection ambiguity once discovered.
options.why: Deferral reduces loaded context but does not remove equivalent operations or clarify the distinct permission semantics encountered after discovery.

options.text: Replace the genuine aliases with one clear published-catalogue operation and retain separately authorized operations for unpublished and archived assets.
options.why: Consolidation follows semantic equivalence, while different asset-state permissions remain explicit rather than being hidden inside a newly broad interface.

questions.decision: Capability reduction should remove accidental duplication, not erase meaningful permissions. Consolidate only the equivalent published operations, describe the remaining distinctions clearly and validate selection on representative tasks. Deferred discovery or stronger prompting cannot by itself repair a tool catalogue whose operations have ambiguous semantics.

video_evidence.concept: Remove overlapping capabilities while preserving meaningful tool distinctions

questions.title: A local transport migration changes the boundary
questions.stem: A chemistry team moves its catalogue integration from a per-user local stdio MCP process to a shared protected HTTP service. The old process received each scientist’s downstream credential through protected local configuration. Engineers plan to copy that environment arrangement into the shared deployment and expose it to all clients. Which TWO design reviews are required before this transport migration is accepted?

options.text: Preserve stdio behavior by accepting any HTTP client that can reach the host, since the underlying tools have not changed.
options.why: Network reachability is not authorization for a protected shared service and does not preserve the original per-user local trust boundary.

options.text: Require every client to supply an arbitrary bearer token and treat any nonempty value as equivalent to the local environment credential.
options.why: A syntactic token presence check establishes neither authenticity, audience nor scope and cannot reproduce the prior downstream authority safely.

options.text: Include the old credential in each tool description so clients can reproduce the same catalogue authority without another authentication step.
options.why: Model-visible definitions expose the secret and cannot establish which caller may use the protected service or the downstream catalogue.

options.text: Define per-user downstream authority or an explicitly scoped service identity, preventing one copied catalogue credential from granting every scientist its privileges.
options.why: The transport change does not authorize credential sharing; downstream access needs an explicit identity and scope model for the shared service.

options.text: Implement and test the protected HTTP service’s MCP authorization contract, including intended resource audience and the caller’s permitted scopes.
options.why: Moving to a shared protected HTTP boundary introduces client-to-service authorization obligations that local process credential provisioning did not satisfy.

questions.decision: Transport migration is also a trust-boundary migration. For a protected HTTP deployment, implement its authorization contract and separately define downstream credentials. The stdio guidance concerns provisioning a local process; it does not permit copying one user’s authority into a broadly reachable shared service.

video_evidence.concept: Stdio credential provisioning differs from protected HTTP MCP authorization

questions.title: A vault needs an egress contract
questions.stem: A managed research agent uses an opaque vault placeholder that is substituted with a catalogue key at outbound egress. The key should remain unreadable to sandbox code. Integration tests discover that an approved diagnostic endpoint echoes request headers and a token-exchange endpoint returns a reusable token in its response. Which THREE changes most directly protect the intended credential boundary while keeping ordinary catalogue queries working?

options.text: Limit secret substitution to the catalogue authentication header and approved destination rather than substituting throughout arbitrary outgoing payloads.
options.why: Narrow host-and-field substitution limits where the secret can be materialized and reduces unneeded exposure while preserving the intended authenticated query.

options.text: Restrict sandbox network destinations independently and test hostile requests against both outbound substitution and inbound response handling.
options.why: Substitution eligibility and network reach are distinct controls; adversarial tests exercise the complete path instead of assuming a vault blocks every misuse.

options.text: Remove or mediate header-echo and token-exchange responses so reusable credentials cannot flow back into the sandbox through permitted endpoints.
options.why: Egress substitution alone cannot prevent a destination from returning the secret or a derived credential in readable response data.

options.text: Rotate the key after each session and retain unrestricted echo responses because short-lived secrets do not count as sandbox-readable credentials.
options.why: Rotation reduces lifetime but does not satisfy the stated unreadability boundary when active credentials can still return through readable responses.

options.text: Keep substitution broad and rely on a prompt prohibition against printing authentication headers, since the model never receives the original key.
options.why: The endpoint response can reveal an active secret regardless of its original absence from context; prompt wording does not enforce that boundary.

questions.decision: Vault substitution protects a specific crossing, not every consequence of authenticated traffic. Constrain where substitution occurs, control permitted response paths and restrict network reach independently. This extends the video’s egress lesson with the official caveat that echoed headers or token responses can make credentials readable inside the sandbox.

video_evidence.concept: External egress credential injection avoids ordinary sandbox secret storage

questions.title: Do not infer the cause from a bundled retrieval change
questions.stem: A standards assistant changes top K from eight to forty while also replacing its ranker. Quality falls from 92 to 89 percent and p95 rises from 2.0 to 3.1 seconds; the release misses both required gates. Engineers assert that extra context alone caused the quality loss. The prior release remains available. Which next step BEST respects the observed accuracy-latency regression while testing the claimed mechanism rather than treating a bundled comparison as causal proof?

options.text: Restore the feasible baseline and compare top-K settings with the ranker held fixed, examining evidence recall and complete-path latency on the same cases.
options.why: The bundle fails its gates, but the experiment cannot isolate context count from ranking; a controlled comparison tests the proposed cause without continued exposure.

options.text: Raise top K further because a replacement ranker needs more candidates, accepting the existing quality and latency misses until its behavior stabilizes.
options.why: This expands an already infeasible configuration without evidence that more context repairs quality or a defined basis for tolerating the missed gates.

options.text: Keep the new ranker and forty chunks, lower model effort until p95 recovers, and attribute the original quality loss to context dilution.
options.why: Another changed component may affect quality and still does not isolate why the bundled retrieval release regressed under the original comparison.

options.text: Revert only top K to eight and declare excess context proven causal if quality improves, without measuring which evidence the new ranker returns.
options.why: A useful rollback trial still needs controlled case-level evidence and cannot justify a broad mechanism claim from one uncontrolled production improvement.

questions.decision: The observed release is worse and should not remain exposed under failed gates. Diagnose which change matters using controlled top-K comparisons with ranking held fixed and evidence-level traces. This qualified extension preserves the chapter’s accuracy-latency lesson while avoiding an unsupported claim that more context alone caused a bundled regression.

video_evidence.concept: More retrieved context must demonstrate quality value against its latency cost

questions.title: Represent a fan-in without inventing parentage
questions.stem: A habitat-report pipeline batches independent upload jobs into one queue message. A worker processes the batch, then emits per-upload results that are joined into separate reports. Traces currently attach the whole batch to whichever upload was enqueued first, making other reports appear to lack extraction. Which TWO instrumentation changes best preserve the actual many-to-one and one-to-many relationships while keeping source content out of propagation metadata?

options.text: Put each full uploaded record in the queue trace headers so downstream spans can reconstruct relationships by comparing record contents.
options.why: Raw content is unnecessary propagation data and comparison is an unreliable substitute for explicit nonsecret identifiers and causal context.

options.text: Duplicate the entire worker trace under every upload and report each copy as an independent execution for latency and cost accounting.
options.why: Duplicated traces falsely multiply shared work and distort expense attribution instead of modeling the actual batch relationship and item-level results.

options.text: Assign the oldest upload as the permanent trace parent and compare report timestamps when investigating missing extraction relationships.
options.why: Choosing one parent plus timestamps reproduces the attribution gap for other contributing uploads and is unreliable under concurrent workload.

options.text: Propagate stable per-upload identifiers into result messages and reconnect each report assembly span to its corresponding extraction result context.
options.why: The fan-out needs item-level correlation so downstream reports retain the correct causal path after shared batch processing completes.

options.text: Carry each contributing upload’s trace context and represent batch consumption with explicit causal links rather than an arbitrary single-upload parent.
options.why: A batch has multiple contributing operations; trace links preserve those relationships without falsely presenting one upload as the sole cause.

questions.decision: Queue propagation must preserve the real causal graph, including batch fan-in. Use links for multiple contributors and item-level correlation for fan-out results. This is a qualified extension of the chapter’s propagation lesson; it requires explicit instrumentation rather than assuming ordinary parent-child tracing automatically models shared batch work.

video_evidence.concept: Trace context must survive queue boundaries

questions.title: Page on sustained user-visible harm
questions.stem: A language service retries transient overload responses. Over the last hour, one region saw 120 provider errors but only two late user requests; another saw twelve provider errors and 600 missed completion deadlines because retries exhausted the queue. The on-call policy currently pages on every provider error. Which replacement BEST aligns alerting with meaningful service harm while keeping raw overload events available for diagnosis?

options.text: Page once for each retry attempt instead of each original error so operators can see the full effort spent recovering requests.
options.why: Retry-level paging increases noise and still does not distinguish harmless recovery work from sustained failures experienced by users.

options.text: Page on sustained completion-failure and deadline-budget consumption by region, retaining provider errors and retry metrics as diagnostic dimensions.
options.why: User-visible symptoms distinguish recovered transient errors from queue-driven harm, while regional signals keep a good aggregate from concealing a damaged slice.

options.text: Page only when the total number of provider overload responses exceeds the first region’s historical peak for an hour.
options.why: Provider-event totals can miss severe user harm in the lower-error region and retain the wrong proxy as the alert trigger.

options.text: Remove overload events from telemetry and page only after users file enough complaints to establish that automatic retries failed.
options.why: Removing diagnostic evidence and relying on complaints delays detection and cannot quantify the sustained deadline failures already visible in service metrics.

questions.decision: Use service symptoms and a defined time window for paging, with provider errors retained as diagnostic evidence. The two regions demonstrate why event count alone misranks harm. Choose thresholds with the service owner and test the alert path rather than claiming one universal threshold suits every workload.

video_evidence.concept: Alert on sustained error-rate and latency harm instead of isolated events

questions.title: A deletion must survive out-of-order delivery
questions.stem: A document assistant consumes source events into keyword and vector indexes. Withdrawal events remove a document, but an older update event occasionally arrives later and recreates its chunks. A cache can also retain the old result. Source events include document identity and monotonically increasing revision numbers. Which TWO changes best prevent resurrection while keeping legitimate later republication possible under a new approved revision?

options.text: Invalidate serving caches by document identity and test delayed-update replay across both indexes and cached retrieval results.
options.why: Deletion must cover every serving path; replay tests verify that index ordering and cache invalidation jointly prevent stale evidence returning.

options.text: Increase deletion priority in the queue while accepting every update event once it arrives, regardless of its revision number.
options.why: Faster withdrawal processing does not prevent a delayed older update from arriving afterward and reversing the intended state.

options.text: Retain versioned tombstones and reject add or update events older than the most recent applied document-state revision.
options.why: A durable ordering rule prevents delayed pre-withdrawal updates from recreating serving content while permitting explicitly newer authorized source state.

options.text: Schedule a complete reindex monthly and rely on the source system to remove resurrected documents at the next full refresh.
options.why: A later rebuild leaves a known serving window for withdrawn evidence and does not prevent older events recreating content between refreshes.

options.text: Remove the document identifier from withdrawn chunks so later updates create a separate record that ranking can distinguish from the old one.
options.why: Discarding identity breaks reliable withdrawal and cache tracking, creating duplicates instead of enforcing the authoritative document-state transition.

questions.decision: Synchronizing deletions requires an ordering model, not merely a delete handler. Keep a tombstone at the applied revision, reject stale events and invalidate all serving copies. This original event-ordering extension preserves the chapter’s core lesson while making later authorized republication an explicit newer state rather than an accidental resurrection.

video_evidence.concept: RAG synchronization must process withdrawals across serving indexes

questions.title: Query the aggregation semantics directly
questions.stem: Operators ask a power-monitor assistant for the highest five-minute mean load between 13:00 and 14:00 local time on the day clocks move backward. The metric store retains UTC samples and supports explicit aggregation windows. A daily narrative summary contains one approximate peak. Which retrieval plan BEST answers the actual numeric question reproducibly while ensuring the ambiguous local interval is resolved before the authoritative query executes?

options.text: Retrieve the daily summary and ask the model to interpolate the five-minute peak from the narrative’s approximate highest observed value.
options.why: A narrative approximation lacks the sample and window information needed to calculate the requested maximum of five-minute means reproducibly.

options.text: Search dashboard annotations for the local time string and use the largest matching number as the peak for the requested interval.
options.why: Text matches cannot establish which repeated interval applies or whether a matching number uses the required five-minute mean aggregation.

options.text: Resolve the intended timezone offset or both repeated intervals, query the metric store with explicit UTC windows, and return the aggregation definition.
options.why: The direct query preserves time and numeric semantics; clarifying the repeated interval prevents a precise calculation over the wrong period.

options.text: Query every sample from the day and ask the model to choose an interpretation of the repeated hour before calculating the peak.
options.why: This leaves an unresolved domain ambiguity to generation and unnecessarily substitutes model arithmetic for the metric store’s explicit time-window aggregation.

questions.decision: Numeric time-series questions need the authoritative store and explicit aggregation semantics. Resolve ambiguous local time before translating it to query windows, and expose the operation used. This goes beyond the chapter’s simple metric lookup by specifying a real ambiguity that direct retrieval alone would not settle.

video_evidence.concept: Structured time-ranged numeric questions require the metric store

questions.title: Resolve a follow-up without freezing a stale premise
questions.stem: A horticulture conversation first asks about irrigation guidance for coastal nurseries. Later, the user says they have moved inland and asks whether the earlier winter exception still applies to them. The retrieval service receives only the final sentence, while an experimental rewriter blindly copies the original coastal constraint. Which TWO query-rewrite behaviors best restore the current meaning and maintain an inspectable basis for the eventual answer?

options.text: Concatenate the first question and last sentence without resolving the intervening correction, since retaining more original text preserves user intent.
options.why: The unprocessed context contains conflicting locations and does not determine which constraint governs the current applicability question.

options.text: Build the standalone query from current conversation state, replacing the superseded coastal location with the explicitly supplied inland condition.
options.why: A rewrite must resolve the present referent and constraints rather than preserve a historical premise the user has explicitly changed.

options.text: Rewrite the follow-up as a general question about winter exceptions and discard location so retrieval can discover all possible interpretations.
options.why: The user has supplied the current location; discarding it weakens retrieval and removes the constraint necessary to assess applicability.

options.text: Retain the exception’s source reference as a candidate to verify against retrieved inland guidance, exposing unresolved applicability instead of assuming transfer.
options.why: The earlier exception identifies the question but does not establish that it applies under the changed location; retrieval must verify that relationship.

options.text: Reuse the previously retrieved coastal passages because a follow-up must be answered from the same evidence as its original question.
options.why: A follow-up can change material conditions, so previous passages may identify the exception without supporting its current applicability inland.

questions.decision: Query rewriting reconstructs the current question, including corrections. Preserve the source referent but replace superseded constraints and verify applicability using new retrieval. This avoids two different failures: a context-free follow-up and a fluent standalone query that confidently retains an obsolete premise.

video_evidence.concept: Conversational follow-ups need standalone retrieval queries

questions.title: Keep deterministic computation as a tool contract
questions.stem: A publishing service calculates royalties through a vendor endpoint. The endpoint takes contract version, units and territory and returns a signed numeric calculation; it neither plans nor conducts an independent investigation. Several supported agent clients now need that operation. Which integration choice BEST provides shared discovery and a stable calculation boundary without inventing an autonomous collaborator merely because the calculation is supplied by another company?

options.text: Describe the vendor as a specialist agent and send it open-ended royalty objectives, allowing callers to infer missing contractual inputs.
options.why: The vendor supplies a fixed calculation service, so an open-ended delegation contract invents capabilities and ambiguity that the actual endpoint cannot support.

options.text: Give every client the vendor documentation in its system prompt and let each model reconstruct the royalty calculation without external calls.
options.why: Documentation is not execution of the signed source calculation and loses the authoritative result boundary required by the publishing service.

options.text: Create a coordinator agent that calls the endpoint repeatedly until its numerical result agrees with a model-generated royalty estimate.
options.why: An unnecessary agreement loop adds cost and treats an unvalidated model estimate as authority over a deterministic signed calculation.

options.text: Expose a narrowly scoped MCP tool around the deterministic endpoint, preserving input validation, returned calculation identity and application authorization.
options.why: Shared client discovery supports MCP reuse, while the operation remains a bounded tool with deterministic inputs and outputs rather than delegated reasoning.

questions.decision: Match the interface to the operation. Multiple agent clients can justify an MCP wrapper for discovery and reuse, but the underlying deterministic service remains a tool. Preserve its validation and calculation identity; agent-to-agent delegation is appropriate for an actual independently reasoning task owner.

video_evidence.concept: A deterministic vendor API is a tool rather than an autonomous agent

questions.title: Evaluate discovery before argument construction
questions.stem: A materials agent searches a deferred tool catalogue. Queries for tensile fatigue find general material summaries, while the fatigue-test tool is described only by an internal acronym. In controlled trials where the correct tool is preselected, argument construction and result use are accurate. Which TWO changes best target the demonstrated discovery failure without replacing the entire deferred catalogue with always-loaded definitions or confusing discovery with permission enforcement?

options.text: Rewrite discovery metadata with task language, applicable inputs and distinguishing limits so fatigue queries can identify the correct capability.
options.why: The failure is upstream semantic discoverability; clearer metadata connects user intent to the right deferred definition without changing working argument construction.

options.text: Use discovery rank as the authorization decision, allowing the top-ranked tool to access every material dataset needed to answer the query.
options.why: Search relevance does not confer data authority; server-side permissions remain necessary regardless of metadata quality or discovery rank.

options.text: Tighten argument schemas for every material tool because accurate calls with preselected tools prove discovery already returns adequate candidates.
options.why: The trial demonstrates the opposite boundary: execution works when discovery is bypassed, so schema tightening does not target the observed miss.

options.text: Return all material tools for any query containing a technical term and count a successful search whenever at least one tool is returned.
options.why: A broad return policy and trivial success metric obscure whether the needed tool was found and discard much of the intended context advantage.

options.text: Add labeled task-to-tool discovery tests that measure whether the required definition enters the candidate set before selection and invocation.
options.why: Stage-specific tests isolate discovery recall from later behavior, showing whether metadata changes repair the observed missing-tool mechanism.

questions.decision: Instrument discovery as its own stage. The supplied control trial localizes the defect to finding the definition, so improve semantic summaries and measure task-to-tool recall before changing execution. Deferred loading depends on discoverability, while authorization remains a separate enforced boundary after a capability is found.

video_evidence.concept: Progressive discovery depends on informative names and descriptions

questions.title: Cache the invariant core and defer exceptions
questions.stem: A training assistant needs an unchanged 3,200-token tone contract on every request. An optional 18,000-token regional appendix is needed in only four percent of conversations. A proposal defers both behind separate fetches, adding a mandatory round trip before ordinary responses. The selected model supports caching at the core’s length. Which context design BEST fits the observed frequency split while preserving full access to the appendix when it is actually required?

options.text: Keep the invariant tone contract in a stable cacheable prefix and load the regional appendix only for tasks that need it.
options.why: The always-required core earns its upfront presence, while deferring the large uncommon appendix avoids irrelevant context and unnecessary common-path discovery.

options.text: Replace the tone contract with a short generated summary and discard the original to ensure no request needs a mandatory fetch.
options.why: The owner requires the unchanged contract; an unvalidated summary changes that obligation rather than choosing a better placement for required context.

options.text: Keep both documents in the initial prompt and cache them together because caching removes their combined tokens from the context window.
options.why: Caching does not remove tokens from context capacity and the rarely used appendix still consumes attention and input space on ordinary tasks.

options.text: Defer both documents but combine their fetches into one tool so each ordinary request pays only one discovery and retrieval step.
options.why: The mandatory fetch still adds common-path overhead for an invariant required core and loads the rarely relevant appendix unnecessarily.

questions.decision: Progressive disclosure should follow need, not operate as an absolute rule. Put small invariant required context in a reusable prefix and defer substantial occasional material. Verify actual caching and end-to-end behavior. The 3,200-token eligibility is stipulated for the selected model, not asserted as a universal cache minimum.

video_evidence.concept: Small static content needed every request can remain inline and cached

questions.title: Completion depends on the external state
questions.stem: A volunteer scheduling agent passes three local step checks on ninety-eight percent of runs: choosing a shift, formatting a request and producing a confirmation message. Yet a downstream race lets another volunteer take the same slot before commitment. The owner defines success as a committed nonconflicting assignment acknowledged to the correct volunteer. Which primary evaluation metric BEST captures the end-to-end failure that the current step scores conceal?

options.text: Grade confirmation messages for confidence and specificity, counting explicit volunteer and shift identifiers as evidence of a completed assignment.
options.why: A specific message can describe a reservation that never committed; presentation does not establish the authoritative scheduling outcome.

options.text: Measure the share of eligible runs ending in a verified nonconflicting committed assignment with acknowledgment delivered to the intended volunteer.
options.why: This directly checks the external final state and delivery condition that define the owner’s successful task rather than intermediate artifact quality.

options.text: Multiply the three local step pass rates and use the product as the estimated successful-assignment rate for reporting.
options.why: The checks do not observe the downstream race, and multiplying marginal pass rates also assumes an unsupported dependency structure.

options.text: Track average time between the formatted booking request and the confirmation message, flagging only unusually slow runs as unsuccessful.
options.why: Fast failures can still produce prompt confirmations, so timing alone cannot establish a valid nonconflicting committed scheduling state.

questions.decision: Grade the task’s actual completion condition at the authoritative boundary. Local steps can be well formed while the final reservation fails. Count eligible runs once and verify commit plus intended acknowledgment; use step checks to diagnose failures rather than substitute them for end-to-end success.

video_evidence.concept: Agent quality requires task success rather than only step scores

questions.title: A judge needs counterexamples with a denominator
questions.stem: A document judge approved all sixty known-good outputs. The team then adds forty adjudicated bad outputs; it rejects thirty-two and incorrectly passes eight. Product wants to reuse the headline one-hundred-percent good-output agreement as evidence that automatic release is safe. The release owner has not set a tolerated bad-output escape rate. Which TWO conclusions correctly use the additional evidence without claiming an unsupported readiness threshold?

options.text: Ask the release owner to define consequence-sensitive acceptance limits and expand validation with representative hard negatives before granting release authority.
options.why: Observed discrimination needs a scoped risk decision and representative coverage; the sample alone does not establish a universal acceptable threshold.

options.text: Report that eight of forty known-bad outputs escaped, giving a twenty percent false-pass rate on this labeled negative slice.
options.why: The negative denominator measures the previously untested always-pass risk; good-output agreement cannot erase the observed escapes among known failures.

options.text: Repeat the forty bad examples with longer explanations until the judge rejects all of them, then treat the same examples as validation.
options.why: Tuning and validating on the same examples risks overfitting and cannot establish discrimination on unseen representative negative cases.

options.text: Report overall ninety-two-percent agreement and omit the separate bad-output rate because the combined score includes all labeled cases.
options.why: The aggregate hides the consequence-relevant escape behavior and can look strong when the evaluation contains many easy positive cases.

options.text: Declare the judge unusable for any evaluation purpose because observing even one false pass disproves the value of model-based grading.
options.why: Imperfect discrimination limits release authority but can still support triage or monitoring when calibrated and paired with proportionate oversight.

questions.decision: Include negatives and keep their denominator visible. Here the observed false-pass rate is 8/40 = 20 percent, despite perfect acceptance of known-good examples. Readiness requires an owner-defined consequence threshold and unseen coverage. The calculation describes this slice, not a population guarantee or an official exam threshold.

video_evidence.concept: Known bad examples reveal whether a judge can fail incorrect outputs

questions.title: Remove the length cue from judge calibration
questions.stem: A policy-summary judge favors long replies. Investigators construct matched pairs: both contain all required facts, but one adds irrelevant reassuring language. Humans prefer the concise version; the judge prefers the padded one even when order is swapped. The product permits different lengths when facts warrant them. Which intervention BEST corrects the evaluation mechanism without forcing useful long explanations into an arbitrary short-output product constraint?

options.text: Use a longer system prompt for the judge and retain the existing holistic helpfulness score so the assessment becomes more thorough.
options.why: More instructions without explicit relevance criteria leave the demonstrated verbosity cue intact and do not establish improved discrimination against padding.

options.text: Add a short-answer bonus equal to the observed length penalty and deploy it without further labels because the matched pairs establish calibration.
options.why: An unvalidated compensating bonus can reverse the bias and penalize necessary detail; the correction itself needs independent evidence across relevant cases.

options.text: Revise the rubric to score required facts and relevance explicitly, then validate on length-varied matched pairs and independent human labels.
options.why: The rubric targets the spurious preference while preserving legitimate detail; matched validation checks whether the correction actually changes the biased judgments.
