options.text: Truncate every evaluated answer to a fixed length before grading so the judge cannot use the original number of words.
options.why: Truncation can remove required facts unequally and changes the evaluated artifact rather than measuring the quality of complete product outputs.

questions.decision: Correct the judge against the intended quality definition. Separate required content from irrelevant elaboration and validate on matched and unseen cases. The chapter’s rubric lesson can reduce verbosity bias; it does not guarantee that a revised rubric removes every length effect or replaces independent calibration.

video_evidence.concept: Judge rubrics must score required content rather than reward padding

questions.title: Treat a failed experiment as diagnostic evidence
questions.stem: A gardening assistant’s new prompt loses a completed randomized comparison. Case review identifies one pattern: B interprets ambiguous plant nicknames as species names without clarification. Other quality slices are unchanged. The team can modify either clarification guidance or retrieval ranking next, but wants interpretable evidence about the observed failure. Which TWO next steps best support a focused iteration without moving the completed test’s finish line?

options.text: Change retrieval, clarification and model effort together, attributing any gain to the clarification rule because it motivated the iteration.
options.why: A bundled intervention can be tested as a package, but it cannot isolate the claimed causal contribution of clarification guidance.

options.text: Delete ambiguous nickname cases from the next evaluation because they were already examined during diagnosis of the failed experiment.
options.why: Removing the failure class abandons the actual service requirement and prevents the next test from demonstrating that the repair works.

options.text: Record B’s completed result and test a specific clarification-rule hypothesis on fresh ambiguous-name examples with retrieval held fixed.
options.why: This preserves the original outcome and isolates a repair linked directly to the observed nickname ambiguity rather than changing unrelated components.

options.text: Rerun B unchanged on progressively smaller cohorts until the ambiguous-name effect disappears, then publish the most favorable comparison.
options.why: Selective cohort searching does not repair the mechanism and misrepresents the completed experiment by choosing a favorable result afterward.

options.text: Retain ordinary unambiguous cases and conversation-completion outcomes as regression checks when evaluating the clarification-rule candidate.
options.why: A targeted clarification fix can add unnecessary questions, so broader checks establish whether it improves the failure without degrading common work.

questions.decision: A losing test narrows the next hypothesis. Preserve its result, target the ambiguous-name behavior and hold other components stable for causal clarity. Use fresh boundary examples plus ordinary conversation checks. This original clarification case applies the video’s iterative-learning lesson without treating repeated testing as a search for a lucky win.

video_evidence.concept: Inspect failed experiments and test one evidence-based hypothesis

questions.title: Keep the guardrail definition fixed
questions.stem: A controlled assistant trial defines safety violations per eligible conversation, with a stop limit of 0.8 percent. B improves resolution from 81 to 86 percent but records 45 violations among 5,000 eligible conversations. Engineers propose dividing those violations by 12,000 individual turns to keep the rate below the limit. The agreed definition is explicit. Which decision correctly respects the precommitted guardrail and the observed primary-metric gain?

options.text: Continue B because the 0.375 percent per-turn rate falls below the numeric limit, provided both denominators are disclosed afterward.
options.why: Disclosure does not make a different denominator satisfy the agreed conversation-level stopping rule or justify continued exposure after a breach.

options.text: Ship B to fewer users and count only resolved conversations in the safety denominator because unresolved cases were not successful product outcomes.
options.why: Restricting the denominator based on outcome changes the measure and can hide violations in precisely the conversations that failed to resolve.

options.text: Continue until B receives 625 additional violation-free conversations, allowing its cumulative rate to fall below the agreed stopping limit.
options.why: Waiting for favorable dilution ignores the already triggered stop condition and exposes additional conversations while the candidate violates the specified rule.

options.text: Stop B under the agreed rule, report its 0.9 percent conversation violation rate and retain the resolution gain as evidence for a safer revision.
options.why: Forty-five divided by five thousand exceeds the stated guardrail; changing the denominator after observing results would redefine the precommitted safety measure.

questions.decision: The agreed unit is the conversation: 45/5,000 = 0.009, or 0.9 percent, above 0.8 percent. Respect the stop rule, preserve the useful resolution evidence and diagnose a safer candidate. Per-turn arithmetic answers a different question and cannot retroactively satisfy this guardrail.

video_evidence.concept: A primary improvement cannot override a preagreed safety stop

questions.title: Structural validity is only the first date check
questions.stem: A booking tool accepts a strict schema with date, time and timezone strings. Structural rejections disappear, but a request made near midnight books the previous day because the model interprets tomorrow in UTC instead of the user’s timezone. The calendar backend correctly executes supplied values. Which TWO changes address this semantic failure while preserving the benefit of strict argument structure and avoiding unsupported claims that a schema alone understands intent?

options.text: Replace the backend with a larger model that reads the strict arguments and guesses whether they express the user’s likely calendar intention.
options.why: This adds another inference over the same ambiguity rather than supplying the missing reference instant and timezone needed for deterministic validation.

options.text: Change date from a free-form string to a pattern matching four-digit year and two-digit month and day, then remove temporal checks.
options.why: A date-shaped string can still represent the wrong intended day; lexical format constraints do not resolve tomorrow relative to the user.

options.text: Add boundary tests around midnight and clock changes, asserting the committed calendar slot against independently computed expected user-local dates.
options.why: Outcome assertions with independent temporal oracles detect well-formed but semantically wrong bookings and verify the intended repair at the action boundary.

options.text: Resolve relative dates against an explicit request instant and user timezone, validating the resulting calendar date before the booking operation.
options.why: The observed error concerns reference-time semantics rather than JSON structure; explicit temporal inputs and validation target that actual ambiguity.

options.text: Increase the tool retry count whenever the backend accepts a date but the user later reports that the booking day is wrong.
options.why: Repeating an accepted wrong operation cannot establish the intended date and can create additional incorrect reservations instead of repairing temporal interpretation.

questions.decision: Use strict schemas for structure and explicit domain logic for temporal meaning. The request instant, user timezone and relative-date rule define the intended slot. Test committed outcomes at midnight and clock transitions. The chapter’s schema lesson is qualified here: valid arguments are not necessarily the correct arguments.

video_evidence.concept: Precise tool definitions and strict schemas address malformed arguments

questions.title: Tell an empty result from incomplete search
questions.stem: An archive search tool returns an empty list for three distinct outcomes: no matching record, a timed-out shard and an invalid collection filter. The agent repeats the same call even for genuine no-match results and sometimes reports that missing shards prove absence. Which tool-result redesign BEST supplies actionable feedback without treating every empty list as either a retryable fault or a definitive negative finding across the whole archive?

options.text: Return typed status, searched scope, completeness and an actionable error or no-match message, with bounded retries reserved for explicitly transient failures.
options.why: Distinct result states let the agent terminate legitimate no-match work and avoid claiming complete absence when search coverage is incomplete.

options.text: Retry every empty response once automatically and present the second empty list as a complete negative result regardless of underlying status.
options.why: A fixed retry does not repair invalid filters or establish shard completeness, so the final absence claim remains unsupported.

options.text: Return a generic no results sentence for every empty list and instruct the agent never to repeat the same search arguments.
options.why: This may stop loops but incorrectly turns timeouts and invalid filters into apparently definitive no-match results without exposing incomplete search scope.

options.text: Raise the default result limit and silently broaden collection filters whenever no records are returned so every call produces usable context.
options.why: Changing search scope silently can violate the user’s question and still fails to distinguish a true absence from a failed shard.

questions.decision: Tool feedback should describe what happened and what remains possible. Explicit status and completeness let the agent choose clarification, bounded retry or a supported no-match response. This extends the chapter’s empty-result lesson: a clear sentence is helpful, but it must not mislabel partial failure as complete absence.

video_evidence.concept: Explicit no-match feedback prevents meaningless repeated tool calls

questions.title: Coalesce evidence without losing its qualifications
questions.stem: A biodiversity assistant retrieves eight overlapping spans from one field protocol. All eight carry useful source identifiers, but repeated text triples context length. The compacted candidate coalesces overlapping spans once and retains citation offsets; an aggressive alternative keeps only central sentences and drops conditional footnotes. The exhibit shows held-out results. Which optimization BEST removes context waste while preserving the required rule qualifications rather than treating the smallest input as automatically best?

options.text: Use central sentences but restore the eight original source labels, assuming valid labels compensate for omitted qualifiers in generated explanations.
options.why: Correct labels cannot supply footnotes absent from context or make an unqualified rule semantically faithful to its actual source conditions.

options.text: Pilot overlap coalescing with preserved offsets and footnotes, retaining regression checks that each quoted rule keeps its applicable qualification.
options.why: Coalescing removes duplicated representation while preserving the evidence contract; the aggressive version violates the explicit qualification requirement despite its lower token count.

options.text: Keep every original overlapping span because changing source representation necessarily invalidates citations even when offsets and source identity are retained.
options.why: Validated offset mappings can preserve verifiable citations; redundant overlapping text need not remain merely because the evidence has stable source identities.

options.text: Deploy the shortest candidate because eliminating the most tokens is the objective once overall answer quality is unchanged on average.
options.why: The qualification failures are a required quality defect, so aggregate parity does not make the smallest representation eligible for this task.

questions.decision: Optimize representation rather than simply deleting evidence. Coalescing overlapping spans can remove repeated text while preserving footnotes and citation offsets. Validate those mappings and required qualifications on held-out cases, then stage deployment. The chapter’s trimming lesson supports removing waste with quality checks, not choosing the fewest tokens regardless of semantic loss.

video_evidence.concept: Remove unnecessary retrieval context only while preserving evaluated quality

questions.title: A pooled percentile can hide a release slice
questions.stem: An assistant’s overall p95 remains under its target after a release. The new prompt serves only four percent of traffic in one language, and almost all of those requests are slow. The aggregate mean is also stable. Request logs already contain feature, model and prompt version but dashboards discard those dimensions. Which TWO monitoring changes most directly expose this regression without claiming that component percentiles can be added into a service percentile?

options.text: Display end-to-end latency distributions by language, feature and resolved prompt/model revision with request counts for each relevant slice.
options.why: The affected four-percent slice can disappear below the pooled p95 boundary; slice distributions and denominators expose the concentrated release regression.

options.text: Add p95 and p99 completion latency for the affected slice and compare pre-release and post-release cohorts under matched workload conditions.
options.why: Tail and version comparisons target the user-visible slowdown while cohort context avoids attributing workload changes to the prompt without supporting evidence.

options.text: Increase the smoothing interval on the global mean so the low-volume language contributes a stable signal across several months.
options.why: Longer aggregation further conceals the affected slice and cannot make a pooled mean diagnose a concentrated tail regression promptly.

options.text: Log only requests slower than the target and remove successful cases because every relevant diagnosis concerns the slow tail.
options.why: Without the successful denominator and workload distribution, the dashboard cannot estimate slice rates or distinguish a population shift from degradation.

options.text: Calculate service p99 by summing the p99 values of retrieval, inference and rendering for every prompt version in the dashboard.
options.why: Component quantiles do not generally add to the service quantile because stage durations have dependencies and different per-request ranks.

questions.decision: Preserve the dimensions that describe the deployed experience and its distribution. A four-percent affected population can remain invisible to pooled p95. Use end-to-end percentiles, slice counts and version comparisons; component spans explain where time goes but their quantiles cannot simply be summed into a service promise.

video_evidence.concept: Monitoring needs configuration breakdowns and tail percentiles

questions.title: Reconcile the cache categories before blaming traffic
questions.stem: A service’s token expense rises after a prompt deployment although request count and output tokens are unchanged. The exhibit records usage per representative request under a stipulated rate schedule: ordinary input costs one unit per thousand tokens, cache reads 0.1 and writes 1.25. There are no writes in either row. Which diagnosis and input-cost comparison are directly supported, before investigating why the cache behavior changed?

options.text: Input cost rises from 2.8 to 12.5 units because every zero-read request must be charged as a cache creation.
options.why: The usage table explicitly shows no writes; a miss can be ordinary uncached input rather than evidence of a cache creation charge.

options.text: Input cost remains 10 units because both requests contain ten thousand total input tokens and caching affects latency rather than billing.
options.why: The stipulated rate schedule assigns cheaper cache reads, so equal logical input size does not imply equal billed input expense.

options.text: Input cost rises from 2.8 to 10 units per request because 8,000 previously read-cached tokens are now ordinary input.
options.why: Before costs 2 + 8 × 0.1 = 2.8 units; afterward all ten thousand input tokens use the ordinary rate.

options.text: Input cost rises from 2 to 10 units because cache-read tokens are not part of the model input or the billed usage.
options.why: Cache reads remain billable input under the stated schedule; excluding them understates the original expense and misrepresents the context supplied.

questions.decision: Reconcile usage categories before choosing a cause. The observed input expense changes from 2.8 to 10 units, about 3.57 times, because reads became ordinary input. This supports investigating prefix identity and eligibility; it does not prove which deployment change broke reuse, and the rates are fictional stipulated arithmetic.

video_evidence.concept: Usage cache-read fields can reveal a cost regression

questions.title: Test the real cross-tool attack path
questions.stem: A travel-library agent reads uploaded itinerary images and can send a reviewed reading list to a stored recipient. Its text-only jailbreak suite passes. A red-team image hides instructions to change the recipient, and the prototype follows them during list delivery. The owner authorizes sending only to the stored recipient. Which TWO next steps best turn this discovery into evidence about the actual release boundary rather than another text-only prompt check?

options.text: Increase the number of ordinary itinerary-reading examples until overall accuracy exceeds the text jailbreak suite’s already passing result.
options.why: Ordinary accuracy cannot substitute for adversarial outcome checks on the discovered image-to-delivery instruction path and its authority boundary.

options.text: Transcribe the image instruction into plain text and retire the image fixture once the existing text classifier detects the wording.
options.why: A text transcription does not verify handling of the original multimodal path or the tool action that demonstrated the release failure.

options.text: Add a warning to delivered lists stating that uploaded images may contain misleading instructions, keeping destination selection under model control.
options.why: A warning after sending cannot prevent the unauthorized recipient change or restore information already delivered across the wrong boundary.

options.text: Enforce recipient binding outside the model and retest both hostile images and legitimate list delivery before expanding the agent’s access.
options.why: Independent destination validation constrains the consequence even if instruction recognition fails, while positive tests preserve the approved useful workflow.

options.text: Add the image-borne attack and related cross-tool variants to adversarial regression tests that inspect the actual delivery destination.
options.why: The observed path crosses visual input into a side effect, so outcome-based tests must cover that modality and consequential tool behavior.

questions.decision: Red-team the actual enabled modalities and tools, then preserve successful attacks as regression cases. The image matters because the path reached an unauthorized side effect. Fix destination authority outside the model and verify legitimate behavior too; improved prompt recognition alone is insufficient evidence that the delivery boundary holds.

video_evidence.concept: Red teaming must exercise prompt injection and jailbreak behavior

questions.title: Bind a fetch to its allowed purpose
questions.stem: A conservation agent fetches public collection pages. Existing network checks correctly block private addresses and validate redirects. However, a permitted public host accepts arbitrary upload parameters and can receive confidential notes encoded into a query string. The legitimate operation needs only public object pages addressed by catalogue identifier. Which THREE controls best narrow this fetch capability beyond the already tested internal-network protections?

options.text: Prevent sensitive local notes from entering outbound parameters and enforce the permitted request shape in the fetch implementation.
options.why: Network destination eligibility alone does not control the content transmitted to an allowed public host; request validation covers that distinct exfiltration path.

options.text: Keep connection and redirect validation active and test encoded-query, method and alternate-path attempts against the narrowed operation.
options.why: Narrowing business semantics complements the existing network boundary; regression attempts verify that neither layer is lost or bypassed during redesign.

options.text: Log full fetch URLs for weekly review and rely on the source page’s public status to justify continuing unrestricted requests meanwhile.
options.why: After-the-fact review cannot prevent notes being sent and may create another sensitive copy in logs without narrowing the exfiltration capability.

options.text: Replace arbitrary URLs with a catalogue-identifier operation that constructs only the approved public object-page path and allowed query fields.
options.why: A purpose-shaped interface removes arbitrary outbound parameters that can carry confidential content while preserving the specific public catalogue lookup.

options.text: Allow arbitrary query parameters only when the host is public, because successful internal-address blocking proves the fetch cannot leak protected information.
options.why: A public destination can receive confidential data; blocking internal addresses addresses SSRF but does not establish safe outbound request content.

questions.decision: The chapter’s deterministic fetch boundary extends beyond a domain allowlist. Here internal-network defenses already work, so the missing control concerns arbitrary content sent to an allowed host. Use a purpose-specific operation, validate outbound fields and retain the independent network checks. Destination safety and data-flow authority are separate obligations.

video_evidence.concept: Fetch capabilities require deterministic tool-layer restrictions

questions.title: Identify the resolved dependency that changed
questions.stem: A drafting application keeps its prompt, retrieval snapshot and tests unchanged. A provider-supported convenience model alias now resolves to a newer snapshot, and a regression appears in the treatment of uncertain dates. Engineers propose restoring only the application container, which uses the same alias. The provider offers explicit supported snapshot identifiers for this route. Which release control BEST makes rollback meaningful and future model changes reviewable under these conditions?

options.text: Rollback the application image and keep the alias because an unchanged application version guarantees restoration of its original external behavior.
options.why: The external alias can resolve differently under the same image, so this rollback does not necessarily restore the model snapshot that passed testing.

options.text: Keep the moving alias and increase prompt repetition until the uncertain-date examples match, treating the regression as independent of model changes.
options.why: This ignores the observed dependency change and introduces another variable without establishing that the original behavior or broader quality is restored.

options.text: Pin the first snapshot forever and disable model regression tests because a dated identifier guarantees permanent provider availability and stable service behavior.
options.why: Pinning controls migration timing but does not guarantee indefinite availability or remove the need to test supported upgrades and other service dependencies.

options.text: Record and deploy the resolved supported snapshot identifier with the release, testing model migrations and restoring the prior complete configuration when needed.
options.why: The container alone does not fix an alias’s moving target; a complete release identity must include the actual external model dependency.

questions.decision: Where the provider exposes supported snapshots, record the actual model dependency rather than just the alias string. Rollback must restore the configuration that was evaluated. Pinning makes changes deliberate; it does not guarantee eternal model availability, so retain a tested migration process and watch the route’s support lifecycle.

video_evidence.concept: Moving model aliases need version-aware regression and migration controls

questions.title: Distinguish wording variation from decision variation
questions.stem: A seed-storage information assistant gives slightly different prose on repeated requests against a frozen procedure. The owner tolerates paraphrases but requires an identical storage-category recommendation and the same cited applicable rule. Twenty repeated trials show varied wording and two category flips. Which mitigation and evaluation BEST addresses the meaningful consistency requirement without promising bit-for-bit deterministic generation or rejecting harmless stylistic variation?

options.text: Constrain the category and rule-reference fields, ground them in the frozen procedure, and measure repeated decision consistency separately from prose similarity.
options.why: The required invariants concern category and evidence, so separate structured decision checks from wording and test repeated runs on the actual rule boundary.

options.text: Choose the most frequent category from the twenty trials as the permanent answer for every future seed-storage question under the same procedure.
options.why: A modal result for one request does not establish correctness across different seed conditions and can freeze a shared mistaken interpretation.

options.text: Use exact whole-response string equality as the only release criterion, because any textual variation demonstrates a change in the storage recommendation.
options.why: Paraphrases are explicitly permitted; whole-string equality confuses harmless presentation differences with the consequential category flips the owner needs controlled.

options.text: Set a supported sampling parameter to its lowest value and remove repeated tests because deterministic settings guarantee identical recommendations across calls.
options.why: Low randomness does not guarantee complete determinism, and settings support varies; repeated outcome checks remain necessary for the stated consistency requirement.

questions.decision: Define consistency at the business level. Ground and constrain the recommendation and applicable rule, then measure repeated decisions on stable evidence. Allowing paraphrase keeps useful flexibility while detecting category instability. Sampling controls can be evaluated when supported, but cannot replace testing or justify a universal determinism promise.

video_evidence.concept: Grounding and repeated trials manage probabilistic output variation

questions.title: Audit the errors reviewers miss
questions.stem: A financial-literacy assistant drafts educational resource recommendations; staff retain responsibility for final advice. In 1,200 reviewed cases, staff override eighteen drafts. Management calls the low override rate proof of model quality. An independent audit of 120 randomly sampled accepted drafts finds six material omissions, and the sampling design is documented. Which TWO conclusions best evaluate the human-review control without extrapolating a precise population error count from this small audit?

options.text: Subtract the audit omission percentage from the override percentage and report the resulting negative value as net review quality.
options.why: These rates concern different populations and events; subtraction has no defined interpretation as the review control’s accuracy or effectiveness.

options.text: Remove review for routine recommendations because the low observed override count demonstrates that human judgment rarely changes the final result.
options.why: The audit already shows accepted outputs with material omissions, so low intervention alone cannot justify reducing the control’s coverage.

options.text: Report the 1.5 percent override rate separately from the observed five percent omission rate in the audited accepted-draft sample.
options.why: Overrides measure visible intervention, while the audit measures missed errors in accepted work; their different denominators prevent treating them as equivalent quality estimates.

options.text: Require reviewers to override at least five percent of all future drafts so the visible intervention rate matches the sampled omission rate.
options.why: A quota can increase arbitrary changes without catching the actual errors and does not turn a sample omission rate into a required intervention fraction.

options.text: Investigate reviewer instructions and evidence presentation, then remeasure missed-error detection with independently adjudicated challenge cases and ongoing acceptance audits.
options.why: The detected omissions justify examining control effectiveness; independent cases and continued audits can establish whether a redesign improves substantive error detection.

questions.decision: Measure review by both interventions and escaped errors. Eighteen of 1,200 is 1.5 percent; six of 120 audited accepted drafts is five percent in that sample. Report uncertainty and sampling scope, then improve the control against adjudicated omissions. Low override frequency alone cannot establish effective validation.

video_evidence.concept: Human review effectiveness requires override error and audit evidence

questions.title: Geography is one priced boundary
questions.stem: A US research organization has an approved first-party API contract for a supported Claude 4.6-or-later route. Its privacy owner requires US inference for this workload and separately owns storage-residency review. The published route price applies a 1.1 multiplier for US inference. A baseline token forecast is $8,400 before that multiplier, with all other charges unchanged. Which budget and compliance statement correctly scopes the architectural recommendation?

options.text: Budget $8,400 because geography affects only routing, and mark all storage locations compliant once the inference flag is set.
options.why: This ignores the explicitly stipulated pricing multiplier and overstates the scope of an inference-location control to unrelated retained data.

options.text: Budget $9,240 for the stated token forecast and verify storage and other data flows separately with the privacy owner.
options.why: The stipulated multiplier adds $840 to token expense, while inference location alone does not establish residency of every retained artifact or service.

options.text: Budget $16,800 because a dedicated inference region always doubles every charge and automatically supplies the organization’s required contractual coverage.
options.why: Neither the stated multiplier nor the scoped control supports doubling cost or treating routing as proof of all contractual obligations.

options.text: Budget $9,240 and treat the multiplier as including a guarantee that prompts, traces and support exports never leave the selected geography.
options.why: The arithmetic is correct but the compliance claim extends beyond the inference-location requirement and must be assessed separately for each data flow.

questions.decision: Apply the scoped published multiplier: $8,400 × 1.1 = $9,240. Then distinguish inference placement from storage and other processing. The privacy owner supplies the actual obligations; the architect implements and evidences them. Pricing and availability are route- and date-sensitive, not universal rules for all partner platforms.

video_evidence.concept: Inference geography can have a route-specific price premium

questions.title: A compliant route is not inherited by every feature
questions.stem: A US clinic’s counsel confirms that HIPAA applies to a planned PHI workflow and owns the BAA determination. The clinic has an approved eligible inference route under a signed BAA, but a new document-persistence feature was not included in the service review. A developer assumes that sharing the same API hostname makes it covered. Which next action BEST implements the established legal ownership and actual service boundary before PHI enters the new feature?

options.text: Use the persistence feature because the clinic already signed a BAA somewhere in the provider relationship and no new company is involved.
options.why: An existing BAA does not prove every feature is eligible or correctly configured; actual coverage must match the proposed service boundary.

options.text: Remove the clinic name from documents and proceed without review because the remaining clinical content cannot be PHI without that identifier.
options.why: Removing one identifier does not establish de-identification or eliminate counsel’s confirmed PHI scope for the proposed workflow and retained clinical records.

options.text: Map the persistence feature’s PHI handling and obtain confirmation of its coverage under the applicable BAA and enabled configuration before use.
options.why: Coverage concerns actual services and features, not hostname similarity; the architect provides data-flow evidence while counsel owns the contractual determination.

options.text: Enable zero retention on ordinary inference and assume it also disables the new persistence feature’s explicit document-storage behavior automatically.
options.why: Inference retention settings do not establish the contract or behavior of a separate persistence feature whose purpose includes retaining documents.

questions.decision: Follow the actual PHI path through each feature. An approved inference route is useful evidence but does not automatically authorize new persistence behavior. Supply counsel with the feature’s storage and access facts, confirm scoped coverage and configuration, and test that only the approved path receives PHI.

video_evidence.concept: HIPAA readiness depends on the eligible route features and BAA

questions.title: A fairness estimate needs the missing outcomes
questions.stem: A rural training programme uses an assistant to explain course eligibility; people decide enrollment. Its fairness dashboard shows equal answer accuracy across regions, but labels come only from completed feedback forms. Forty percent of rural sessions and five percent of urban sessions lack outcome labels, often after connection loss. The owner wants equitable information access and transparent limits. Which TWO changes best address what the current dashboard can actually establish before claiming regional parity?

options.text: Explain the evaluated population and current coverage limits, provide a usable support and correction route, and verify it works under poor connectivity.
options.why: Transparency must describe the evidence limits and offer an actionable route for affected users rather than presenting a conditional dashboard result as universal assurance.

options.text: Report parity unchanged because accuracy is equal among labeled sessions, treating missing feedback as evidence that the remaining users found the answer sufficient.
options.why: Missing feedback can reflect connection loss rather than satisfaction; the unequal coverage makes that inference unsupported by the observed respondent-only data.

options.text: Replace regional comparisons with overall answer accuracy and remove discussion of coverage limits so users receive one clear quality statement.
options.why: Pooling conceals the known coverage disparity and removing limits undermines transparency rather than establishing equitable outcomes for poorly connected users.

options.text: Investigate label missingness and sample outcomes independently of feedback completion, comparing regional error and task-completion rates under a documented evaluation design.
options.why: Equal accuracy among respondents does not establish parity for sessions missing labels; independent coverage can reveal selection effects and actual access failures.

options.text: Collect more completed feedback forms through the same online flow and declare fairness once both regions have identical numbers of labeled responses.
options.why: Equal sample counts do not repair a completion-dependent selection mechanism that systematically excludes different proportions or types of sessions by region.

questions.decision: Fairness measurement depends on who is observed. Respondent-only parity cannot establish parity when missing outcomes differ substantially across regions. Investigate coverage with independent sampling and task-completion evidence, then explain the evaluated scope and provide a usable challenge route. This extends the chapter’s measurement lesson to selection bias rather than a renamed matched-attribute case.

video_evidence.concept: Fairness needs group-aware measurement and transparent contestability

questions.title: Explain absence without a fabricated confidence number
questions.stem: A coastal-history assistant receives a question about whether an undocumented vessel stop proves a family’s migration route. The archive has gaps, and the assistant cannot inspect private collections. Current answers confidently infer the route from the absence of contrary records. The owner wants a useful, transparent research service rather than a generic disclaimer. Which response policy BEST communicates the actual evidential limit and gives the researcher an actionable next step?

options.text: Add a ninety-percent confidence label to the inferred route and retain the same explanation because numerical uncertainty is more transparent than caveats.
options.why: An uncalibrated percentage gives false precision and does not explain which collections were missing or why absence fails to establish the route.

options.text: Refuse every migration question because incomplete archives prevent certainty, even when documented stops support a clearly bounded partial answer.
options.why: Complete refusal discards useful verified evidence when the service could provide a scoped partial answer with explicit gaps and research directions.

options.text: Return only the retrieved vessel names and remove all explanation, since a shorter factual list avoids the need to describe limitations.
options.why: The researcher still needs to understand the relation between evidence and inference; omitting explanation does not resolve the misleading absence-based conclusion.

options.text: Distinguish documented stops from inference, cite searched collections and their gaps, and suggest an archivist or additional records for unresolved routes.
options.why: The response makes the evidence boundary understandable and directs further investigation without converting an incomplete search into a confident historical conclusion.

questions.decision: Transparency should describe what the evidence establishes and what the service could not assess. Cite the searched scope, separate facts from inference and provide a concrete escalation or research path. This extends the chapter’s health example to historical evidence without importing medical advice or relying on arbitrary confidence numbers.

video_evidence.concept: Transparent answers state limitations sources and qualified escalation

questions.title: Discover freshness at the decision instant
questions.stem: A theatre assistant recommends seats from a nightly availability export. Discovery finds that reservations change every minute, but the recommendation only becomes binding when a separate checkout service commits it. The business owner permits clearly labeled indicative suggestions and requires live validation before purchase. Which requirement BEST captures freshness without unnecessarily insisting that every explanatory sentence query the live inventory service or allowing stale availability to become a promise?

options.text: Document indicative suggestion freshness and require authoritative availability revalidation at checkout, with explicit sold-out handling before a binding purchase.
options.why: The requirement ties freshness to the actual commitment boundary while preserving the owner-approved use of labeled indicative information during earlier browsing.

options.text: Replace the nightly export with an hourly export and guarantee suggested seats remain available because the shorter interval reduces average staleness.
options.why: More frequent export still cannot guarantee minute-changing inventory at commitment and ignores the owner’s explicit live-validation requirement.

options.text: Require every generated sentence to use a live lookup and remove checkout validation because all earlier answers then use current inventory.
options.why: Earlier reads can become stale before commitment; excessive lookup frequency does not replace authoritative validation when the purchase actually becomes binding.

options.text: Require users to refresh the assistant conversation before checkout and treat their refreshed message as proof that seat availability remains current.
options.why: A refreshed conversation does not query authoritative inventory or establish availability at the actual purchase boundary where the business requires validation.

questions.decision: Discovery should turn source volatility into a requirement at the relevant decision boundary. Here the owner permits indicative browsing but requires live checkout validation and sold-out handling. Record both contracts. This qualified extension avoids equating freshness with one universal refresh interval or assuming an earlier live read guarantees later availability.

video_evidence.concept: Discovery records data freshness requirements that shape integration

questions.title: Communicate the residual risk after review
questions.stem: A board reviews an archive assistant pilot with 400 adjudicated responses. Twelve initial drafts contained material errors; reviewers caught nine before delivery, and three reached users. The pilot covered one language and excludes handwritten records. Directors ask whether human review makes the system error-free. Which communication BEST states the measured result and its limitations without presenting pilot frequencies as a guarantee for all future work or hiding the residual risk?

options.text: Report ninety-nine-point-two-five percent accuracy and promise the same rate in every language because human reviewers remain part of the architecture.
options.why: The percentage describes this delivered pilot sample; the limited population and observed review misses do not support a universal future guarantee.

options.text: Explain the three-percent draft error rate and 0.75-percent delivered-error rate, name excluded inputs, and describe monitoring and escalation for the remaining risk.
options.why: The answer separates model errors from review escapes, states the actual pilot denominator and exposes coverage limits instead of implying that review eliminates mistakes.

options.text: Avoid error rates because the pilot is small, showing only the number of positive curator comments and the names of current reviewers.
options.why: Sample limits should qualify measured evidence rather than replace it with testimonials that cannot describe the observed draft and delivered error behavior.

options.text: Report that review caught seventy-five percent of errors and describe the system as safe, omitting delivered-error frequency until a second pilot confirms it.
options.why: The caught fraction is useful but omitting the observed escapes hides the board’s central residual-risk question and overstates the control’s effectiveness.

questions.decision: Communicate the whole error path: 12/400 = 3 percent draft errors, nine caught, and 3/400 = 0.75 percent delivered errors. Explain what the pilot excluded and how residual failures are handled. These are observed frequencies with uncertainty, not guarantees or a promise that the next model release removes review escapes.

video_evidence.concept: Executives need measured error limits and controls rather than perfection claims

questions.title: Make the dispute an observable comparison
questions.stem: Two engineers disagree about evidence chunk size. One favors paragraph chunks and one favors page chunks. The evaluation corpus currently contains only short documents, although the dispute concerns footnotes spanning page boundaries in long reports. Both proposals use the same model and budget. Which evidence package BEST supports an architectural decision without settling by seniority, choosing an arbitrary midpoint or treating an unrepresentative benchmark win as decisive?

options.text: Present published chunk-size defaults from several frameworks and adopt the most common value because external consensus replaces local workload uncertainty.
options.why: Framework defaults do not measure this corpus’s cross-page evidence relationships or the actual complete-path latency and cost tradeoffs.

options.text: Run both on the existing short-document set and select the statistically clearer winner because controlling dataset changes is more important than coverage.
options.why: A precise comparison on the wrong population cannot settle the long-report footnote failure that motivates the architectural choice.

options.text: Compare both on adjudicated long-report boundary cases plus ordinary traffic, reporting supported answers, retrieval coverage, end-to-end latency and total cost.
options.why: The comparison addresses the disputed mechanism and preserves representative coverage, allowing stakeholders to assess quality and economics on the actual target workload.

options.text: Choose the midpoint of average paragraph and page lengths, recording both engineers as co-owners so the decision fairly represents their experience.
options.why: A compromise size and shared ownership do not provide evidence that the boundary condition or the service requirements are met.

questions.decision: Turn disagreement into a controlled workload comparison. Include the specific cross-boundary evidence relation and ordinary requests, hold unrelated configuration fixed and report complete-path tradeoffs. The result gives stakeholders a reasoned choice while retaining the limits of the evaluated population; no chunk size is universally superior.

video_evidence.concept: Architectural disagreements should be settled with comparable evaluation evidence

questions.title: Separate acceptance from the next investment
questions.stem: A translation pilot met signed exit criteria for terminology preservation, reviewer effort and cost. At the acceptance meeting, the sponsor asks for real-time voice translation and says acceptance should wait until that capability works. The original contract covers documents only, and the voice use case introduces a new latency and consent regime. Which response BEST respects the achieved pilot evidence while giving the sponsor a concrete route to evaluate the new business need?

options.text: Declare the voice request out of scope and close the engagement without documenting it because the original acceptance criteria were already met.
options.why: This preserves the old boundary but fails to manage a legitimate new stakeholder need through an accountable change process and decision path.

options.text: Fold voice into the pilot’s existing quality score by counting document translations as successful voice cases until a prototype is available.
options.why: This redefines the measured artifact and misrepresents document evidence as proof of an unevaluated capability with materially different operating requirements.

options.text: Delay acceptance without changing the record, implementing voice informally so the sponsor can approve both capabilities under the original evidence package.
options.why: An informal expansion obscures scope, owners and acceptance conditions and cannot make the original document evaluation validate the new voice behavior.

options.text: Record document-pilot acceptance against its agreed criteria and open a separately scoped voice change with owners, feasibility evidence and new acceptance measures.
options.why: The response preserves truthful reporting of completed work while treating the new modality and its constraints as a reviewable change rather than retroactive failure.

questions.decision: Keep acceptance tied to the agreed artifact and criteria, then evaluate the new need through change control. Voice introduces different requirements and cannot inherit document-pilot evidence. A concrete next decision can welcome the sponsor’s goal while preserving an accurate account of what the completed pilot actually established.

video_evidence.concept: New goals are explicit changes rather than retroactive pilot criteria

questions.title: Acknowledge is not the same as restore
questions.stem: A regional archive agrees that severe assistant incidents must be acknowledged within fifteen minutes. The support team’s dashboard stops timing when an automated email is sent, but the service owner meant a responsible operator accepts the incident. Some reports remain unattended for hours. Which TWO agreement changes best make support performance observable without promising an identical fix time for every possible defect or confusing a receipt with accountable response?

options.text: Promise a fifteen-minute permanent fix for every severe incident so acknowledgment and resolution can use the same simple completion event.
options.why: A universal permanent-fix promise is unsupported by capacity or failure complexity and erases the meaningful difference between response and resolution.

options.text: Track restoration or resolution objectives separately by severity, recording exclusions, customer updates and ownership when a permanent fix requires longer investigation.
options.why: Separating response from recovery makes commitments realistic and inspectable while maintaining accountable communication throughout an unresolved incident.

options.text: Measure only average incident lifetime across severities because pooled timing is easier to compare than separate response and restoration indicators.
options.why: Pooling hides the severe unaccepted reports and cannot show compliance with the owner’s explicit response boundary and severity-specific expectations.

options.text: Keep the automated receipt definition and shorten its target to one minute so the acknowledgment metric better reflects urgency to customers.
options.why: Faster receipts still do not establish that a responsible operator has accepted and begun handling the incident under the intended agreement.

options.text: Define acknowledgment as acceptance by the staffed responsible role, with a measurable start event, severity classification and escalation when unaccepted.
options.why: The definition matches the owner’s intended control and removes the ambiguity that allowed an automated receipt to masquerade as operational response.

questions.decision: Define the event the promise actually concerns. An email receipt differs from a staffed acceptance, and both differ from restored service or permanent resolution. Specify severity, timing, owners and escalation, then measure each relevant obligation separately. The concrete fifteen-minute target comes from the service agreement, not a universal support standard.

video_evidence.concept: Support objectives define acknowledgment and resolution by severity

questions.title: An explicit non-goal needs a handoff
questions.stem: A municipal information assistant explains permit requirements, while inspectors determine compliance and approve permits. Partner teams interpret an architecture diagram’s response arrow as permission to issue approvals and begin building that feature. The approved service scope excludes approval authority. Which documentation addition BEST prevents this misinterpretation and gives implementers a useful boundary rather than merely restating that the assistant answers questions or adding more internal component detail?

options.text: State that permit approval is excluded, show the inspector handoff and define response contracts that distinguish informational guidance from authoritative disposition.
options.why: Scope plus a concrete handoff and interface semantics translates the non-goal into implementable behavior instead of leaving authority implicit in a diagram.

options.text: Add a disclaimer to the development team’s chat channel while leaving the architecture document and response schema as they currently stand.
options.why: An ephemeral message is unlikely to guide future implementers and does not repair the authoritative documentation or the ambiguous interface contract.

options.text: Add every possible future approval feature to a roadmap appendix so partner teams can infer which authority might eventually move into the assistant.
options.why: A speculative roadmap can deepen scope ambiguity and does not define today’s excluded authority or the required inspector handoff.

options.text: Expand the model and retrieval boxes in the diagram with implementation classes, leaving the response arrow and scope narrative unchanged.
options.why: Internal detail cannot resolve the partner teams’ mistaken interpretation of external approval authority or specify the intended operational boundary.

questions.decision: Non-goals become useful when they connect to observable behavior. Explicitly exclude approval, document the responsible human handoff and distinguish guidance from disposition in the interface. This extends the chapter’s scope lesson into an implementation contract so teams can build the authorized service without guessing where its authority stops.

video_evidence.concept: Architecture guidance needs explicit scope and non-goals

questions.title: Draw the system at the right abstraction
questions.stem: A museum board wants to understand who supplies collection evidence, who uses a public assistant and which external services receive data. A separate security session will examine internal storage and network controls. The current proposal shows database tables and every inference call, obscuring the museum’s organizational boundary. Which diagram BEST answers the board’s present question while leaving room to link to detailed engineering views separately?

options.text: Show every deployment container and its compute region so the board can infer user groups and information exchanges from network placement.
options.why: Deployment placement supports a different engineering review and forces nontechnical readers to infer the actor and service relationships they explicitly asked to see.

options.text: Show the assistant as one bounded system with user groups and external services, labeling relationships by purpose and exchanged information.
options.why: A system context view exposes actors, neighboring systems and interactions without burying the organizational question in internal implementation detail.

options.text: Show the exact sequence of retrieval, inference and rendering calls for one sample request, omitting actors not involved in that example.
options.why: A single request sequence can miss other relationships and emphasizes temporal internals rather than the complete system environment the board requested.

options.text: Show all database entities and foreign-key relationships because every external interaction must eventually be represented in a persisted data model.
options.why: An entity model answers internal data-structure questions and does not clearly communicate the people and external services surrounding the assistant.

questions.decision: Choose the view for the question. A system context diagram shows the assistant boundary, people and neighboring services with meaningful relationship labels. Link deeper sequence, container or deployment views when their questions arise. More implementation detail does not automatically make a stakeholder picture more informative or complete.

video_evidence.concept: A system context diagram explains users and external systems

questions.title: Verify ownership across the alert chain
questions.stem: An assistant is handed to a rotating operations team. The on-call address receives infrastructure alerts, but a quality-regression detector still opens tickets assigned to the architect’s inactive account. A dashboard appears green because it tracks notification transmission rather than acceptance. Which TWO handoff changes best establish accountable quality-incident response without broadcasting sensitive examples to every user or assuming delivery proves the receiving team can act?

options.text: Route quality tickets to the staffed operations queue with a named escalation owner and appropriate access to protected diagnostic evidence.
options.why: The actual response path needs both accountable ownership and usable evidence; a successful notification to an abandoned account cannot provide either.

options.text: Forward every quality ticket to all assistant users so whichever recipient first notices a problem can decide whether to investigate.
options.why: Broadcasting does not create responsibility and can expose protected evidence to people without the role, access or ability to contain the incident.

options.text: Exercise a synthetic quality incident through detection, assignment, acknowledgment and containment, recording receiving-team acceptance and gaps before handoff completion.
options.why: An end-to-end rehearsal verifies the operational chain rather than just message delivery, exposing permissions or ownership failures while builders can still repair them.

options.text: Keep the architect assigned permanently and add a reminder to check the old account before holidays because historical expertise is the strongest control.
options.why: A personal dependency remains a fragile ownership path and does not transfer accountable operational responsibility to the team that now runs the service.

options.text: Suppress tickets until the quality detector is fully accurate, relying on infrastructure alerts to represent service health during the handoff period.
options.why: Quality regressions can occur with healthy infrastructure; suppressing their path removes coverage instead of establishing response ownership for a fallible detector.

questions.decision: Handoff includes quality operations, not only infrastructure notifications. Assign the real staffed queue, grant appropriate evidence access and exercise the full acknowledgment-to-containment path. This applies the chapter’s alert-routing lesson while checking that the receiving owner can respond; delivery counts alone do not establish operational readiness.

video_evidence.concept: Monitoring alerts must transfer to the operating team at handoff

questions.title: Rank improvement hypotheses by observed harm
questions.stem: A deployed assistant has three improvement proposals: a visual redesign requested by senior staff, a rare-language retrieval fix linked to repeated harmful omissions, and a broad model upgrade with no diagnosed target. The language slice is small, so raw complaint totals understate its high failure rate. The product owner wants evidence-led iteration with limited capacity. Which prioritization method BEST combines impact and uncertainty without reducing the decision to popularity or total request volume?

options.text: Allocate equal effort to each proposal so every stakeholder sees progress, postponing evaluation until all three changes can be released together.
options.why: Equal allocation ignores observed consequence and repair evidence, while a combined release weakens attribution of both improvements and regressions.

options.text: Implement the model upgrade first because a general capability increase can be assumed to address all three proposals without separate diagnosis.
options.why: A broad upgrade has no established connection to the observed omissions and may introduce cost or regressions without demonstrating the intended improvement.

options.text: Rank hypotheses using affected-user harm, slice failure rates, reach and repair evidence, then test the highest-priority candidate with explicit acceptance gates.
options.why: This combines consequence and exposure with a concrete repair hypothesis, preventing small high-impact populations from disappearing behind raw volume or stakeholder prominence.

options.text: Rank proposals only by total complaint count because population-level frequency is the most objective measure of every improvement’s business impact.
options.why: Raw counts obscure the concentrated harmful omission rate and do not represent severity, affected population or the evidence supporting a proposed repair.

questions.decision: Prioritize a tested hypothesis rather than an attractive component or loud request. Use monitoring, slice denominators and observed consequences to estimate impact, then assess whether the repair targets the mechanism. Small populations can justify high priority when harms concentrate there; record the decision and validate before expanding deployment.

video_evidence.concept: Iteration priorities come from monitoring evaluation and user evidence

questions.title: Permit the registry without opening every host
questions.stem: A Claude Code project’s sandboxed shell can reach the approved package registry but dependency installation fails when the registry redirects tarball downloads to its documented artifact CDN. Bash permission already permits the package command. The team has verified the CDN’s intended domain and needs only those artifacts. Which configuration change BEST restores the legitimate workflow while retaining the sandbox network boundary rather than treating command approval as network authorization?

options.text: Put the CDN hostname in CLAUDE.md and retain the existing network policy because repository instructions override sandbox connection denials.
options.why: Context instructions do not change the enforced sandbox network configuration and cannot grant a shell process access to a blocked destination.

options.text: Disable sandbox networking restrictions for the entire installation session and rely on the registry URL to constrain every subprocess and redirect.
options.why: A starting URL does not bound subprocess destinations or redirects, and disabling the boundary is broader than the verified artifact-download need.

options.text: Add a broader Bash allow pattern for the package command because command permissions automatically authorize every network destination the process contacts.
options.why: Bash command approval and sandbox network restrictions are distinct; expanding the command rule does not authorize the blocked CDN destination.

options.text: Add the verified artifact CDN domain to the sandbox network policy, retaining the registry rule and testing installation with unrelated destinations still blocked.
options.why: The failure concerns a required network destination, so a narrow host-policy change addresses it while preserving the independent command permission and egress boundary.

questions.decision: Inspect the destination actually needed by the package workflow. Add only the verified CDN domain to the sandbox network policy and test both successful installation and continued blocking elsewhere. The chapter’s empty-list example generalizes to incomplete allowlists; command permission and network access remain distinct controls.

video_evidence.concept: Sandbox network policy must permit required package registry destinations

questions.title: Learn the execution path before changing it
questions.stem: A new engineer needs to understand how an unfamiliar image-processing repository handles a corrupt input. Documentation lists modules but not the error path. Claude Code can inspect the repository and run isolated local tests. The engineer’s first deliverable is a reviewed onboarding note, not a refactor. Which workflow BEST uses the coding assistant to establish an evidence-based mental model while retaining teammate knowledge that the source alone may not explain?

options.text: Trace one corrupt-input path through entry point and tests, draft file-linked architecture notes, and review assumptions and business rationale with a maintainer.
options.why: A concrete execution path grounds the note in code while maintainer review supplies historical or business context that inspection cannot independently establish.

options.text: Have the assistant replace maintainer onboarding with a generated FAQ and treat unanswered business questions as implementation defects to fix later.
options.why: Code assistance cannot recover every unwritten rationale, and treating missing historical context as a defect misrepresents the repository and the onboarding goal.

options.text: Ask for a full architecture summary from filenames alone, publishing it immediately because a broad overview is more useful than a narrow error trace.
options.why: Filenames do not establish execution behavior, and an unreviewed broad summary can turn plausible module guesses into misleading onboarding guidance.

options.text: Rewrite the error handler into a familiar design before reading its tests so the engineer can learn the system through immediate structural improvement.
options.why: The deliverable is understanding, and premature changes can remove important behavior before the engineer knows the repository’s requirements and current guarantees.

questions.decision: Use code exploration to answer a concrete behavioral question and cite the path that supports the explanation. Draft notes remain hypotheses where source evidence is incomplete; a maintainer can confirm rationale and unstated constraints. The result is a reviewable onboarding artifact rather than an ungrounded architectural narrative or premature rewrite.

video_evidence.concept: Claude Code supports code-grounded exploration and reviewed onboarding notes

questions.title: Give an independent reviewer an independent oracle
questions.stem: A coding assistant changes a laboratory file parser. A second session reviews the patch, but it receives the author’s design narrative as its main evidence and never reads the stated compatibility contract. Both sessions approve silently changing a missing measurement to zero. The team wants independent review that tests the intended behavior. Which THREE workflow changes best address shared assumptions while preserving a useful author explanation as supporting material?

options.text: Give the second session the same conversation and ask it to use a harsher tone so agreement is less likely to look deferential.
options.why: A tone change does not supply an independent oracle or remove the shared assumptions that caused both sessions to miss the compatibility violation.

options.text: Accept the patch when two sessions agree and all author-written tests pass, treating session count as the independent-review acceptance criterion.
options.why: Agreement and copied tests can reproduce one mistaken premise; neither establishes compliance with the missing-value contract the reviewers failed to inspect.

options.text: Keep final merge authority with the accountable team and require resolution of material reviewer findings with reproducible evidence before integration.
options.why: A separate session supplies critique, not automatic approval authority; accountable resolution ensures identified contract violations actually affect the integration decision.

options.text: Ask the reviewer to identify counterexamples and run independently specified missing-value fixtures, including downstream aggregation behavior affected by the distinction.
options.why: Independent oracles and downstream checks can expose a semantically wrong but locally passing implementation rather than mirroring the author’s tests.

options.text: Give the reviewer the patch, compatibility contract and repository evidence in fresh context, separating author claims from the review’s required acceptance criteria.
options.why: Independent review needs an external correctness basis; fresh context helps only when the reviewer can judge the patch against actual requirements.

questions.decision: Independent review needs separate judgment and independent criteria. Fresh context reduces author anchoring, but the reviewer still needs the contract, relevant code and tests whose expected behavior is grounded outside the patch. A second model’s approval is evidence to assess, not a substitute for accountable integration authority.

video_evidence.concept: A separate fresh-context coding reviewer reduces author-session blind spots

questions.title: Make the incident repair reviewable before execution
questions.stem: During an indexing incident, Claude Code proposes a production database repair that updates records matching a broad status predicate. New records may enter that status while approval is pending. The incident owner permits an emergency audited change, but requires a human to approve the exact affected population and a recoverable execution plan. Which change package BEST satisfies that authorization before the operator uses the approved production path?

options.text: Run a read-only count for approval and execute the same predicate later without row identity checks, assuming the count establishes population equivalence.
options.why: Equal counts can contain different records, and a later predicate may affect newly matching rows despite the same reported population size.

options.text: Prepare an explicit versioned row manifest, reviewed update and recovery plan, then execute with precondition checks that stop if approved state changed.
options.why: The package makes the affected population reviewable and prevents a drifting predicate from silently extending approval to newly matching production records.

options.text: Apply the generated update directly with a database administrator credential and ask the incident owner to inspect the changed rows before closing the ticket.
options.why: Post-execution inspection cannot provide the required prior authorization or a pre-reviewed recovery plan for a consequential production data change.

options.text: Review the status predicate alone and run it repeatedly until no matching rows remain, because the incident approval covers the repair’s intended purpose.
options.why: A purpose-level approval does not authorize an expanding population when the owner specifically requires exact affected rows and recoverable execution.

questions.decision: Turn an incident suggestion into a concrete change artifact before execution. Bind approval to the exact rows and relevant versions, provide recovery and stop when preconditions differ. The chapter’s human-approved normal path applies even under urgency; an emergency process can be fast while preserving its defined authorization and audit boundaries.

video_evidence.concept: Production incident changes need human approval and the audited execution path

drills.title: Control boundaries under changing evidence
drills.stem: Judge each proposal independently against its stated requirement. These supplemental exercises are unscored; no fixed number of Yes answers is implied.

rows.text: Requirement: no withdrawn document may reappear after delayed ingestion. Proposal: delete serving chunks once but accept later updates regardless of revision.
rows.why: A delayed pre-withdrawal update can resurrect the document without a retained ordering rule or tombstone.

rows.text: Requirement: a critic assesses causal support independently. Proposal: provide source excerpts and the draft but omit the author’s persuasive conversation.
rows.why: This retains evidence needed for judgment while reducing anchoring on the generator’s self-justification.

rows.text: Requirement: a maker’s tiny mark remains readable. Proposal: replace shelf originals with a contextual thumbnail and a validated high-detail mark crop.
rows.why: The targeted representation can reduce irrelevant visual input while preserving the task’s distinguishing detail.

rows.text: Requirement: the sandbox cannot read an active API secret. Proposal: allow an authenticated diagnostic endpoint to echo substituted secret headers into responses.
rows.why: An outbound substitution boundary does not prevent the endpoint from returning the secret to the sandbox.

rows.text: Requirement: approval covers an exact production row set. Proposal: preserve a row-version manifest and stop execution if its preconditions no longer match.
rows.why: The reviewed population and state remain bound to execution rather than expanding through a drifting predicate.

drills.title: Conclusions from the stated measurements
drills.stem: Decide whether each conclusion follows from the evidence. Judge every row independently; equivalent wording need not imply an equivalent decision.

rows.text: A judge rejects 27 of 30 known-bad responses. Its observed false-pass rate on that negative slice is ten percent.
rows.why: Three bad responses pass out of thirty known-bad responses; 3/30 is 10 percent.

rows.text: Only four percent of requests use a slow prompt. A healthy pooled p95 proves this prompt meets its own latency target.
rows.why: A small affected population can lie beyond the pooled p95 boundary and needs its own denominator and distribution.

rows.text: Every case takes three review minutes; one quarter additionally takes twelve. For 800 cases, expected human work is 4,800 minutes.
rows.why: The mean is 3 + 0.25 × 12 = 6 minutes, multiplied by 800 cases.

rows.text: A strict booking schema accepts tomorrow as a correctly formatted date field. This alone proves the date matches the requester’s timezone.
rows.why: Structural compliance does not resolve relative-date reference time or the intended local calendar day.

rows.text: An alias still has the same string after container rollback. This alone proves the application returned to the prior resolved model snapshot.
rows.why: A convenience alias can resolve to a different supported snapshot independently of the application image.

drills.title: Choose the missing lifecycle evidence
drills.stem: Match each need to the artifact whose primary purpose addresses it. Choices may repeat; all rows are supplemental and unscored.

rows.text: Specify how index consumers reject a pre-withdrawal event arriving after the withdrawal revision.
rows.why: The needed artifact defines authoritative revision ordering and permitted serving-state transitions.

rows.text: Record which ranker was held fixed when comparing eight versus forty retrieved chunks.
rows.why: Controlled factors and candidate configurations belong with the evidence supporting the comparison.

rows.text: Define when a staffed incident acknowledgment starts and which role accepts responsibility.
rows.why: The ambiguity concerns the measurable support commitment and its accountable owner.

rows.text: Show public visitors, curators and external catalogue services around a single assistant boundary.
rows.why: The requested view concerns actors and neighboring systems rather than internal execution details.

rows.text: Preserve the held-out qualification cases supporting overlap coalescing rather than central-sentence extraction.
rows.why: Case definitions, results and tested representation differences document the optimization evidence.
